license: Compiled from publicly published manufacturer specifications, national/EU legal standards, and standard brewing literature. Each record carries its own sourceUrl and attribution — check those before redistributing. This export deliberately excludes the recipe archive, which is community-contributed content subject to a takedown policy.

notes.fermentables: PPG is points per pound per US gallon. Where ppgBasis is 'nutrition', the value is derived from the product's Nutrition Facts panel as 46 x (totalCarbG - fiberG) / servingSizeG; the inputs are included so the arithmetic can be checked.
notes.hops: Alpha/beta acids vary by crop year and lot — these are typical published ranges, not a lot analysis.
notes.water: All ion values are ppm (mg/L). Municipal supplies vary seasonally; these are historical/representative profiles.
notes.yeast: cellsPerUnit is billions of viable cells per pack/vial/gram.
notes.additives: effectPerGramPerLitre is what one gram per litre does to the named metric - signed, so deacidifiers are negative. Acids move titratable acidity roughly 1:1; DAP delivers 212 mg/L YAN per g/L by stoichiometry. Dose ranges are typical practice, not limits: check your own jurisdiction's legal maxima for sulphite and sorbate.
notes.legalStandards: Our own summaries of statutory and protected-designation standards (beer purity law, sake classification, cider appellations, spirits standards of identity). Summaries, not legal advice — check the current instrument for your jurisdiction. Third-party judging guidelines (BJCP, Brewers Association, AWS) are deliberately excluded from this export.
notes.fermentationArchetypes: How yeast is handled for each family of drink — beer by cells/mL/degree Plato, wine and cider by grams per hectolitre, sake and baijiu by starter culture, many traditional drinks spontaneously or with no yeast at all. Every numeric figure carries the sourceUrl it came from (AWRI, OIV, Scott Laboratories, peer-reviewed literature). Where researchStatus is 'pending' the approach is described but no figure is asserted — that is a deliberate gap, not a missing value to be filled in with a guess. Each guideline category carries an 'archetype' key naming the record here that governs its ferment.

yeastLabs.name: Angel Yeast Co.
yeastLabs.description: One of the world's largest yeast producers; dominant in distilling/ethanol and Chinese baijiu, with growing fruit-wine, mead, and beer lines. Many high-temperature, high-alcohol-tolerance distilling strains.

yeastLabs.name: Bacteria & Mixed Cultures
yeastLabs.description: Souring bacteria and mixed fermentation cultures. These are not yeast — they are lactic and acetic acid bacteria that produce acid rather than (much) alcohol, plus the blended cultures that combine them with Saccharomyces and Brettanomyces. Catalogued at species level, which means most numeric specs are deliberately null: a species does not have a temperature range, a product does. Where a figure appears it comes from a named commercial datasheet for a specific product, and that product is named in the entry.

A species does not have a fermentation temperature range — a commercial strain does — so numeric specs here are null unless a named datasheet for a named product supplies them, in which case the product is named in the entry. Everything else is described in prose with the figure attributed to whoever published it.

yeastStrains.name: Lactobacillus plantarum
yeastStrains.description: The workhorse of kettle souring. Lallemand's WildBrew Sour Pitch is a L. plantarum product and its datasheet is the source of the figures here: 30-40 °C, reaching pH 3.2-3.5, pitched at 10 g/hL. The datasheet classifies it as a facultative hetero-fermentative strain and specifies unhopped wort. Produces little alcohol itself.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Citrus, tangy, sour (WildBrew Sour Pitch datasheet descriptors).
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: The datasheet's temperature range is given for unhopped wort, so sour before any hop addition. The recommended dose is 10 g/hL and the product is specified at >10^11 CFU/g. This entry deliberately states no IBU inhibition threshold: an earlier version of this record claimed '5-8 IBU', which the datasheet does not say and which was not sourced.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Lallemand WildBrew Sour Pitch — Technical Data Sheet
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: species, 30-40 °C, pH 3.2-3.5, 10 g/hL, >10^11 CFU/g, flavour descriptors, style list, unhopped-wort requirement. Does not support: attenuation, alcohol tolerance, flocculation, or any IBU threshold — all null.
yeastStrains.attribution: Every numeric field in this file traces to one of three named documents, recorded per strain in specBasis/sourceTitle/sourceUrl: the Lallemand WildBrew Sour Pitch technical data sheet (vendor spec for a specific product); Vriesekoop et al. 2012, '125th Anniversary Review: Bacteria in brewing: the good, the bad and the ugly', Journal of the Institute of Brewing 118:335-345 (peer-reviewed); and the Maltose Falcons homebrew club's 'Brewing Sour and Wild Ales' (club guide). Qualitative behaviour is attributed the same way. Fields no source supports are null rather than estimated.

yeastStrains.name: Lactobacillus brevis
yeastStrains.description: The most hop-tolerant of the common lactic acid bacteria, and for that reason the classic beer-spoilage organism as well as a deliberate souring culture for long mixed-culture ageing rather than quick kettle souring. Vriesekoop et al.'s review identifies it as among the most hop-resistant and most commonly implicated beer-spoilage LAB; hop iso-alpha-acids act as ionophores that collapse the proton motive force, and hop resistance is what lets L. brevis survive them.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Lactic acidity. This entry no longer claims a specific funk development curve, which was unsourced.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: A genuine spoilage risk in clean beer — segregate soft equipment (tubing, gaskets, buckets). No temperature, alcohol-tolerance or IBU figures are given here: the cited review establishes relative hop resistance qualitatively but does not publish a species-wide numeric range, and strain variation is large.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Vriesekoop et al. (2012), 125th Anniversary Review: Bacteria in brewing — the good, the bad and the ugly, J. Inst. Brew. 118:335-345
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: relative hop tolerance, spoilage significance, mechanism of hop inhibition. Does not support: any temperature range, alcohol tolerance, attenuation or IBU threshold — all null. Previous version asserted 20-35 °C, 8% ABV and '10-15 IBU' with no source.

yeastStrains.name: Pediococcus damnosus
yeastStrains.description: The slow, deep souring organism of traditional Belgian sour beer, and with L. brevis one of the two lactic acid bacteria most often responsible for beer spoilage. The Maltose Falcons' club guide describes its working behaviour: it produces large amounts of lactic acid from glucose, produces no CO2, and the early stages of the ferment carry a massive charge of diacetyl.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Deep lactic sourness; heavy diacetyl (butterscotch) during the process, per the Maltose Falcons guide.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Expect a ropy phase and heavy diacetyl early on. Both are described as normal stages by the club guide, which pairs Pediococcus with Brettanomyces so the Brett cleans up what the Pedio leaves. Do not dump it on the strength of the ropy phase. No temperature or alcohol-tolerance figures are asserted — neither cited source publishes them for this species.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Maltose Falcons Homebrew Club — Brewing Sour and Wild Ales (Pediococcus section); hop-tolerance and spoilage context from Vriesekoop et al. 2012, J. Inst. Brew. 118:335-345
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: lactic from glucose, no CO2 production, massive early diacetyl charge, Brett pairing. Does not support: temperature range, alcohol tolerance, attenuation — all null. Previous version asserted 16-29 °C and 10% ABV with no source.

yeastStrains.name: Acetobacter
yeastStrains.description: The 'vinegar mother'. It converts ethanol into acetic acid, which is what makes vinegar, and it needs oxygen to do it — that oxygen dependence is the whole control lever. In a sealed, topped-up vessel it does very little; in a barrel with headspace or a leaking bung it takes over.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Vinegar, sharp acetic bite. This entry no longer quantifies an ethyl acetate threshold, which was unsourced.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Almost never pitched deliberately in beer. Control it by controlling oxygen: keep vessels full and sealed. No temperature range is given — the cited sources describe the organism's role and oxygen requirement but publish no range.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Maltose Falcons Homebrew Club — Brewing Sour and Wild Ales ('Acetobacter — Vinegar Mother — converts ethanol to acetic acid'); brewing-spoilage context from Vriesekoop et al. 2012, J. Inst. Brew. 118:335-345
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: ethanol-to-acetic-acid conversion, role as spoilage/complexity organism. Does not support: temperature range — null. Previous version asserted 16-32 °C with no source.

yeastStrains.name: Lambic / Mixed-Culture Blend (generic)
yeastStrains.description: The traditional consortium, sold commercially as blends — the Maltose Falcons' guide names White Labs WLP655 Belgian Sour Mix, Wyeast 3278 Belgian Lambic Blend and Wyeast 3763 Roeselare Blend. Saccharomyces ferments the sugars first, Lactobacillus and Pediococcus acidify, and Brettanomyces works slowly on what the others leave behind.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Barnyard funk, lactic tartness, leather. Character development is slow — see the timeline below.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: The club guide's own timeline: expect at least a month before the cultures show any character at all, and optimally six months to a year to let the beer bloom. Use dedicated soft equipment and keep this culture away from clean beer. This entry no longer claims a '1-3 year, three-for-gueuze' schedule or a specific 1.000 finishing gravity — those figures were not sourced.

yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: the consortium's composition and division of labour, the named commercial blends, and the 'at least a month / six months to a year' timeline. Does not support: attenuation, temperature, alcohol tolerance, terminal gravity — all null.

yeastStrains.name: Lactobacillus delbrueckii
yeastStrains.description: Produces lactic acid for a crisp, dry acidity and is the primary souring character of Berliner Weisse. The Maltose Falcons' guide gives the one figure recorded here: ferment it very warm, on the order of 98 °F (37 °C).
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: The cited guide gives a single warm target (~98 °F) rather than a range, so only the minimum is populated here and the maximum is null. Do not read the 98 °F figure as an upper limit.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Maltose Falcons Homebrew Club — Brewing Sour and Wild Ales (Lactobacillus section)
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: lactic acid production, crisp dry acidity, primary character of Berliner Weisse, warm ferment ~98 °F. Does not support: an upper temperature bound, alcohol tolerance, attenuation — all null.

yeastStrains.name: Brettanomyces lambicus
yeastStrains.description: The Brett of lambic — the Maltose Falcons' guide associates it with 'every lambic' and describes it as the biggest Brett character of the three commonly used species.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Huge 'horsey' Brett character with some fruitiness, plus smoky and sour flavours (Maltose Falcons descriptors).
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Slow. Numeric specs are null: the cited guide characterises the species by flavour and origin, not by temperature, attenuation or alcohol tolerance, and those vary by isolate. An earlier version of this record described it as a 'cherry-pie Brett' with 85-100% attenuation and 12% tolerance; the cherry framing and all three numbers were unsourced.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Maltose Falcons Homebrew Club — Brewing Sour and Wild Ales (Brettanomyces section)
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: association with lambic, 'horsey' character with fruitiness, smoky and sour notes. Does not support: attenuation, temperature, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null.

yeastStrains.name: Brettanomyces claussenii
yeastStrains.description: The softest of the commonly used Brett species. The Maltose Falcons' guide gives its origin as English stock beer and calls it a softer Brett — a reasonable first Brett for that reason.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Pineapple and mango; soft rather than barnyard (Maltose Falcons descriptors).
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Numeric specs are null — the cited guide describes origin and aroma contribution only. Attenuation and alcohol tolerance figures in an earlier version of this record were unsourced.
yeastStrains.sourceTitle: Maltose Falcons Homebrew Club — Brewing Sour and Wild Ales (Brettanomyces section)
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: English stock beer origin, softer Brett character, pineapple/mango aroma. Does not support: attenuation, temperature, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null.

yeastStrains.description: Treated by the Maltose Falcons' guide as closely related to B. claussenii, sharing its softer character rather than the lambic strains' funk.

yeastStrains.name: Brettanomyces bruxellensis (species)
yeastStrains.description: The classic 'Brett' of Belgian sour and wild ales, and the organism behind Brett character in wine. The Maltose Falcons' club guide places its origin in Brussels and describes it as producing a medium amount of the earthy funk associated with Brett — between the softer claussenii and the much bigger lambicus.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Slow — plan in months, not weeks. All numeric specs are null: an earlier version of this record claimed 85-100% attenuation, 16-29 °C and 12% alcohol tolerance while citing a Wikipedia page on the genus, which supports none of those numbers. Attenuation in particular is strain-dependent and depends on how much dextrin the primary yeast left behind.
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: Brussels origin, medium earthy funk, position relative to the other Brett species. Does not support: attenuation, temperature, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null.

yeastStrains.name: Lachancea thermotolerans (as WildBrew Philly Sour)
yeastStrains.description: A yeast that produces both lactic acid and ethanol, souring and fermenting in one step with no bacteria involved. The figures here are the published specification for Lallemand's WildBrew Philly Sour, a pure active dried L. thermotolerans strain — not species-wide values. Its datasheet gives 74-82% attenuation, 20-30 °C (optimal 25-30 °C), high flocculation, 9% ABV tolerance, 50-150 g/hL, and fermentation completable in ten days at 20 °C. The strain is POF negative, diastaticus negative and killer negative.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Sour, red apple, stone fruit, notably peach (WildBrew Philly Sour datasheet descriptors).
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Datasheet pitching rate is 50-150 g/hL, viability at least 1x10^9 CFU/g. Lower temperatures within the 20-25 °C band call for the higher end of that rate. The pH 3.2-3.5 and 0.1-0.4% lactic acid figures the datasheet quotes apply to Lallemand's standard-conditions wort, so treat them as indicative rather than a promise about your wort. An earlier version of this record claimed 70-82% attenuation, 17-28 °C, medium flocculation and 10% tolerance — every one of those four was wrong against the datasheet.
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: every numeric field above, for this product. Does not support: species-wide behaviour of L. thermotolerans, or wine applications — the datasheet is a brewing document.

yeastStrains.name: Torulaspora delbrueckii (species)
yeastStrains.description: A non-Saccharomyces yeast of established interest both as a pure brewing starter and, more commonly, in wine co-fermentation. Michel et al.'s review of pure non-Saccharomyces starter cultures covers it among the species of brewing interest; in winemaking its documented value is lower volatile acidity and increased aromatic contribution when inoculated sequentially before Saccharomyces.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Aromatic contribution with low volatile acidity; the specific ester profile depends heavily on strain and on whether it is used pure or sequentially.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: In wine it is normally inoculated first and followed by Saccharomyces, which is where the volatile-acidity benefit comes from; used entirely alone it will usually stick before a wine ferments dry. Numeric specs are null — the cited review does not publish species-level temperature, attenuation or alcohol-tolerance ranges, and the previous version of this record asserted 60-78% attenuation, 18-28 °C and 9% tolerance on the strength of a Wikipedia species page.
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: standing as a non-Saccharomyces brewing starter, and the low-volatile-acidity/aromatic role in sequential wine fermentation. Does not support: any numeric range — all null. Verification is metadata-only (abstract and search summaries, not full text).

yeastStrains.name: Kluyveromyces marxianus (species)
yeastStrains.description: A fast-growing, genuinely thermotolerant yeast that assimilates and ferments lactose, which most brewing yeast cannot — hence its interest for whey and dairy-based ferments. Fonseca et al.'s review reports maximum growth temperature variously as 47 °C (Anderson et al. 1986), 49 °C (Hughes et al. 1984) and 52 °C (Banat et al. 1992), and ethanol production above 40 °C. Two findings from the same review matter more for anyone thinking of pitching it: its ethanol tolerance is LOWER than that of S. cerevisiae, and it is Crabtree-negative and cannot grow under strictly anaerobic conditions, with ethanol formation almost exclusively tied to oxygen availability.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Fruity and ester-rich; will ferment milk sugar.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: Not a drop-in replacement for a brewing yeast. Because it cannot grow strictly anaerobically and its ethanol formation is oxygen-linked, a conventional sealed, oxygen-free fermentation is the wrong environment for it. No numeric fields are populated: the published maximum growth temperatures disagree (47/49/52 °C) and are growth limits rather than recommended fermentation ranges, so they are reported above with their attributions instead of being averaged into a fake range. The alcohol tolerance is null and deliberately so — an earlier version of this record claimed 10%, which is the figure reported for strains after roughly 100 days of directed adaptive evolution, not a native specification, and it pointed in the opposite direction to what the literature actually says. That earlier version also listed 'Bioethanol' as a recommended style, which is an industrial application and not a drink.
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: lactose assimilation and fermentation, thermotolerance with the three attributed maxima, ethanol production above 40 °C, lower ethanol tolerance than S. cerevisiae, Crabtree-negative character, inability to grow strictly anaerobically. Does not support: any single alcohol-tolerance number, attenuation, flocculation, or a recommended fermentation temperature range — all null.

yeastStrains.name: Saccharomycodes ludwigii (species)
yeastStrains.description: A maltose- and maltotriose-negative yeast: it will not ferment the main wort sugars, so it produces very little alcohol while still generating fermentation aroma. Michel et al.'s review notes that it is the most studied yeast for low- and non-alcoholic beer and that alcohol-free beer is already produced industrially with it, which is what makes it interesting — the low alcohol comes from what the yeast cannot eat rather than from stripping alcohol back out afterwards.
yeastStrains.flavorNotes: Fermentation-derived aroma with very little alcohol; the review's point is that the flavours are desirable rather than merely tolerable.
yeastStrains.optimalPitchNote: The approach works because the sugars are left behind, which means the finished beer is sweet and full of fermentable material — it is microbiologically vulnerable and needs the same care as any low-alcohol product. Numeric specs are null; the cited review does not publish species-level ranges.
yeastStrains.sourceNote: Supports: maltose- and maltotriose-negative character, resulting low alcohol with desirable flavour, industrial use for alcohol-free beer. Does not support: temperature, attenuation, flocculation, alcohol tolerance — all null. Verification is metadata-only.

waterProfiles.name: Burton upon Trent
waterProfiles.description: The most famous brewing water on earth. Enormously high sulfate from the local gypsum accentuates hop bitterness into a crisp, dry, minerally snap — the 'Burton snap' — and made the town the historic capital of pale ale. So influential that adding gypsum to liquor is still called 'Burtonisation'.
waterProfiles.attribution: Classic brewing-city ion concentrations (ppm) compiled from the standard homebrewing literature — Palmer & Kaminski 'Water', the Bru'n Water knowledge base, and A.J. deLange's historical analyses. Municipal water varies seasonally and with treatment; these are the historical/representative profiles brewers target, not a current tap analysis. Style-target profiles follow the Bru'n Water colour-and-balance framework.

waterProfiles.name: Dublin
waterProfiles.description: Very high bicarbonate alkalinity — the reason Dublin became a stout city. Only heavily roasted, acidic dark malts can balance the mash pH this water pushes up, which is exactly what Guinness-style dry stout is built from.
waterProfiles.attribution: Classic brewing-city ion concentrations (ppm) compiled from the standard homebrewing literature — Palmer & Kaminski 'Water', the Bru'n Water knowledge base, and A.J. deLange's historical analyses. waterProfiles.name: Kentucky Limestone
waterProfiles.description: The water that made bourbon country. Filtered through deep limestone, it is hard and alkaline but crucially iron-free — dissolved iron ruins fermentation and blackens whiskey, and the limestone strips it out while adding the calcium yeast love. Not a beer profile, but the reason Kentucky, not somewhere else, became the home of American whiskey.

waterProfiles.name: RO / distilled water
waterProfiles.description: A blank slate: reverse-osmosis and distilled water are effectively free of the six brewing ions, which is exactly why serious brewers use them. Rather than correcting whatever the tap happens to deliver this month, you add the salts you want and know precisely what is in the liquor. Sold in the US as distilled water in gallon jugs and dispensed from supermarket RO machines. These zeroes are not a measurement of a particular brand — they are what the process produces by definition; RO removes roughly 95-99% of dissolved solids and distillation essentially all of it. Build any profile on this page up from here with the salt calculator.
waterProfiles.attribution: Definitional rather than a brand analysis: RO and distillation remove substantially all dissolved minerals, so the starting point is zero on every ion. Empirically confirmed by the bottlers themselves: the distilled-water columns of the Poland Spring, Zephyrhills and Ice Mountain analysis reports return ND (not detected) on every mineral, and Aquafina's California report gives ND for total dissolved solids at a 10 mg/L reporting limit. Purified bottled water in the United States really is this row.

waterProfiles.name: evian
waterProfiles.description: A single-source alpine water from the Cachat spring, and one of the few big brands that publishes a full ion analysis. Very high bicarbonate (360 ppm) against modest calcium makes it alkaline: it will push mash pH up, so it suits dark malty beers that need the carbonate to offset roast acidity, and fights you on pale hoppy ones. Sulfate and chloride are both low, so it carries almost no flavour bias of its own. Stated pH 7.2.
waterProfiles.attribution: Mineral composition as published by evian on its own product page (Ca 80, Mg 26, Na 6.5, Cl 10, SO4 14, HCO3 360 mg/L; also K 1, silica 15, nitrates 3.8; pH 7.2).

waterProfiles.name: Badoit
waterProfiles.description: Naturally sparkling water from Saint-Galmier, and one of the most alkaline waters in common supply: 1250 ppm bicarbonate against only 153 ppm calcium. Do not brew on it neat — that residual alkalinity would leave a pale mash far above target pH. Its use is as a measured carbonate addition to a dark or malty grist, where a small blend supplies the alkalinity roast malt wants without the chalk that famously refuses to dissolve. The 180 ppm sodium is not negligible either: it will read as a soft, faintly salty roundness well before it reaches the level that tastes salty.
waterProfiles.attribution: Composition as published by Badoit (Danone) on its own composition page: HCO3 1250, Ca 153, Na 180, Mg 80, Cl 54, SO4 35, silica 27, fluoride 1.2 mg/L. The page states these are regulatory-analysis values, stable over time.

waterProfiles.name: Gerolsteiner Sprudel
waterProfiles.description: The most heavily mineralised water most brewers can buy off a shelf: 1816 ppm bicarbonate with 348 ppm calcium, from the volcanic Eifel. Like Badoit this is a blending ingredient, not a brewing liquor — but it is a far better one, because it carries its enormous alkalinity together with the calcium a mash actually needs, rather than with sodium. A litre or two into a dark grist does the job chalk is supposed to do and does badly, since calcium carbonate is barely soluble in water while this water arrives with it already dissolved.
waterProfiles.attribution: Analysis excerpt published by Gerolsteiner Brunnen on its own product page (mg/L): hydrogen carbonate 1816, calcium 348, magnesium 108, sodium 118, chloride 40, sulfate 38, potassium 11. The six brewing ions plus potassium balance to within 0.1% on charge, which is what a complete real analysis looks like.

waterProfiles.name: Mountain Valley Spring Water (still)
waterProfiles.description: A rare thing in the United States: a nationally sold bottled water drawn from one spring, with a published analysis you can actually brew to. Moderate calcium against 232 ppm bicarbonate gives a residual alkalinity of about 137, which sits between Munich's and Dublin's — squarely dark-beer territory. With barely 2 ppm each of chloride and sulfate it contributes essentially no flavour bias of its own, so you are free to set the sulfate:chloride balance entirely with salts. Suits dark and malty beers as it comes; a pale beer will need acid.
waterProfiles.attribution: From the 2025 Mountain Valley Water Quality Report, still-water column (mg/L): calcium 65-70, magnesium 6.1-7.2, sodium 1.7-2.5, chloride 1.8-2.5, sulfate 5.2-8.2, total alkalinity as CaCO3 190, TDS 210, pH 7.3-8.1. Midpoints are shown here. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity converted at the standard 1.22 mg/L HCO3 per mg/L CaCO3; the resulting ion set balances to within 0.5% on charge.

waterProfiles.name: S.Pellegrino
waterProfiles.description: The surprise of this table, but read the RA column before you get excited. S.Pellegrino carries 388 ppm sulfate against 51 ppm chloride — a sulfate:chloride ratio of about 7.6:1, the most hop-forward water sold in a supermarket, and the only entry here that pulls bitterness the crisp, dry, minerally way Burton does. It is not Burton, though. Burton's 270 ppm bicarbonate is almost exactly cancelled by its 275 ppm calcium, landing it at a residual alkalinity of about 1; S.Pellegrino has less calcium and lands at about 43, nearer London. So it brews as a sulfate-led pale ale water that still wants acid for a pale grist — or a little gypsum, which raises the calcium and walks it the rest of the way toward Burton. Genuinely brewable neat, unlike the two carbonate waters above it, though 388 ppm sulfate will flatten anything malt-forward.
waterProfiles.attribution: From the 2023 S.Pellegrino Water Analysis Report published by Nestle USA (mg/L): calcium 164, magnesium 46.4, sodium 29.9, chloride 51, sulfate 388, potassium 2.5, total alkalinity as CaCO3 187, total hardness as CaCO3 601, TDS 901, pH 5.18. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 1% on charge.

waterProfiles.name: Volvic
waterProfiles.description: Very lightly mineralised volcanic water: every one of the six ions is in single or low double figures except bicarbonate. That makes it a good base for delicate pale lagers, where real mineral content coarsens the malt. One honest caveat the table makes visible: it is not a Pilsen substitute. Pilsen runs 3 ppm bicarbonate for a residual alkalinity of about -4; Volvic runs 80 ppm with only 13 ppm calcium to offset it, so its RA is about 51 — higher than London's. Soft is not the same as acidic. Brew pale on it and you will still want acid or acidulated malt.
waterProfiles.attribution: Analyse caracteristique published by Volvic (Danone) on its own product page (mg/L): calcium 13, magnesium 9, sodium 12, potassium 7, chlorides 16, sulfates 9, bicarbonates 80, silica 31, nitrates 7.7. The full ion set balances to within 1% on charge.

waterProfiles.name: Poland Spring
waterProfiles.description: The most useful of the big American spring brands, because its range is narrow enough to plan around. Whatever bottle you get, the water is soft and barely alkaline: calcium never exceeds 12 ppm and total alkalinity tops out at 32 ppm as CaCO3, giving a residual alkalinity around 13 at the midpoint and staying low across the whole span. That is close enough to a blank slate to treat it as one - build the profile you want on top and allow for a little alkalinity you did not add. Sulfate and chloride are both single figures, so it carries no flavour bias of its own.
waterProfiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2022 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. Published as a range because the brand is not one water: the report names the several springs it is drawn from and the figures span all of them. The six columns here are the midpoint of that range so the salt calculator has something to work with; the range itself is what the bottler actually measured. Bicarbonate is the published total alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

waterProfiles.name: Ozarka
waterProfiles.description: The softest of the American brands and the one closest to reverse osmosis. Total alkalinity never exceeds 12 ppm as CaCO3 and calcium never exceeds 8.3, which puts residual alkalinity at about 1 - effectively nothing to correct. The catch is chloride, which swings from 3.3 to 37 ppm across the springs; that is a real difference in mouthfeel, and it is the one number you cannot assume. Excellent base water for pale, delicate beers if you treat the chloride as unknown.
waterProfiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2025 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. Published as a range because the brand is not one water: the report names the several springs it is drawn from and the figures span all of them. The six columns here are the midpoint of that range so the salt calculator has something to work with; the range itself is what the bottler actually measured. Bicarbonate is the published total alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

waterProfiles.name: Deer Park
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
waterProfiles.description: Listed as a warning rather than a target. Deer Park's own report gives total alkalinity as 3.1 to 160 ppm as CaCO3 - a fiftyfold spread - with calcium from undetectable to 68 and sulfate from undetectable to 39. One bottle is essentially distilled water and another is a moderately hard, alkaline supply, and nothing on the label tells you which you have. The midpoint shown here is arithmetic, not a measurement, and brewing to it would be guessing. If this is what your shop stocks, use it for cleaning and buy distilled water for the kettle.
waterProfiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2023 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. Published as a range because the brand is not one water: the report names the several springs it is drawn from and the figures span all of them. The six columns here are the midpoint of that range so the salt calculator has something to work with; the range itself is what the bottler actually measured. Bicarbonate is the published total alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

waterProfiles.name: Zephyrhills
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
waterProfiles.description: Florida limestone, and it shows: at the top of its range this is a hard, alkaline water, at the bottom it is nearly soft. Total alkalinity runs 11 to 160 ppm as CaCO3 and calcium 5.4 to 68, so like Deer Park it cannot be brewed to as a number. What you can rely on is direction - every sample leans alkaline rather than acidic, so it will push mash pH up, never down. Treat it as an unknown carbonate water and measure your mash rather than trusting the label.
waterProfiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2021 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. waterProfiles.name: Arrowhead
bestForStyles: Not recommended as a brewing target
waterProfiles.description: The widest-swinging of the western brands: total alkalinity 18 to 190 ppm as CaCO3, calcium 4.2 to 52, magnesium 1.5 to 20. The one thing that stays put is chloride, which never exceeds 5.4 ppm in any sample - unusually low, and the reason Arrowhead tastes lean rather than round. That single stable number is not enough to brew on when everything else moves by an order of magnitude. Distilled water is the better buy from the same shelf.

waterProfiles.name: Ice Mountain
waterProfiles.description: By far the hardest and most alkaline American spring brand, drawn through Michigan limestone: total alkalinity 170 to 320 ppm as CaCO3, calcium 46 to 79, magnesium 16 to 34. The range is wide in absolute terms but never crosses a decision boundary - even the softest sample has a residual alkalinity well over 100, so this is a dark-beer water in every bottle. That makes it more useful than the brands with wider proportional swings: you cannot hit a number, but you can confidently pick a style. Pale beers on it will need a substantial acid addition.

waterProfiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Mount Shasta, CA)
waterProfiles.description: Crystal Geyser bottles from seven springs but, unusually and to its credit, publishes a separate report for each one rather than a single blended range - so a bottle labelled Mount Shasta is a known water. This one is soft and remarkably clean: chloride below 0.76 ppm and sulfate below 1.9, meaning almost no flavour ions at all, over a moderate alkalinity that puts residual alkalinity near 46. Check the label for the source before trusting these figures; the other six springs have their own reports and their own numbers.

From the CG Roxane bottled water report for the Mount Shasta (Weed, California) source. Ranges are that single spring's sampling spread, not a blend of different springs, which is why they are narrow. Bicarbonate is the published alkalinity as CaCO3 converted at 1.22.

waterProfiles.name: Acqua Panna
waterProfiles.description: The most ordinary water in this table, and that is a compliment. Moderate calcium, moderate alkalinity, nothing extreme in any direction: residual alkalinity around 67 and a sulfate:chloride ratio near 3:1 put it naturally in amber and malty-but-not-dark territory, and it is the only brand here you could brew a balanced beer on without adjusting anything. Where S.Pellegrino is an argument and Gerolsteiner is an ingredient, Panna is simply water that happens to suit brewing.
waterProfiles.attribution: From the 2022 Acqua Panna Water Analysis Report published by Nestle (mg/L): calcium 34, magnesium 6.9, sodium 7, chloride 7.5, sulfate 22, total alkalinity as CaCO3 95, total hardness as CaCO3 110, TDS 140, pH 7.7. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 0.1% on charge.

waterProfiles.name: Perrier
waterProfiles.description: A third carbonate water, and the most useful of them for a brewer, because its alkalinity arrives with a lot of calcium and very little sodium - 138 ppm calcium against only 7.8 sodium, where Badoit gives you 180 ppm of sodium for the privilege. Residual alkalinity is about 231, far too high to brew on neat, but that is the point: a measured blend supplies carbonate and calcium together, which is exactly what a dark grist wants and what chalk fails to deliver. Cheaper and more widely stocked than Gerolsteiner, if a little weaker.
waterProfiles.attribution: From the 2024 Perrier Water Analysis Report published by Nestle Waters North America (mg/L): calcium 138, magnesium 3.6, sodium 7.8, chloride 21.2, sulfate 26.4, total alkalinity as CaCO3 332, total hardness as CaCO3 359, TDS 476, pH 5.52. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 3.5% on charge.

waterProfiles.name: FIJI Water
waterProfiles.description: The lowest sulfate of any water here by a distance: 0.6 ppm, against 9 ppm chloride. Nothing else on this page is so completely free of the ion that sharpens bitterness, which makes it a soft, round, malt-leaning liquor whatever else you do to it. Residual alkalinity around 109 points the same way, toward darker and maltier beers. It is also unusually high in silica, the brand's main marketing claim, which has no effect on brewing worth adjusting for.
waterProfiles.attribution: Transcribed from the 2025 Water Analysis Report linked above, the bottler's own certified-laboratory panel. From the FIJI Water Company bottled water quality report (mg/L): calcium 18, magnesium 14, sodium 16, potassium 4.6, chloride 9, sulfate 0.6, alkalinity in CaCO3 units 130, TDS 220. Bicarbonate is the alkalinity converted at 1.22; the ion set balances to within 0.1% on charge, the tightest in the table.

waterProfiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Johnstown, NY)
waterProfiles.description: The hardest and most alkaline of Crystal Geyser's springs, and the only one with real chloride in it: 30 ppm against 12 ppm sulfate, so it leans distinctly malty and round before you add anything. Residual alkalinity near 102 makes it a dark-beer water as it comes. The closest thing here to a domestic Munich, and much easier to buy.
waterProfiles.attribution: From the CG Roxane bottled water report for this named spring. Crystal Geyser publishes a separate report per source rather than one blended range, so a bottle labelled with this spring is a known water. The report prints an 'Alkalinity' and a 'Bicarbonate' row carrying the same figure, which cannot both be right — bicarbonate in mg/L is 1.22x alkalinity as CaCO3, never equal to it. Charge balance settles it: read as alkalinity as CaCO3 and converted, the ion set balances; read as bicarbonate directly it is out by roughly 20%. So the figure is treated as alkalinity and converted. Published (mg/L): calcium 58, magnesium 11, sodium 12, chloride 30, sulfate 12, alkalinity 150.

waterProfiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Norman, AR)
waterProfiles.description: Arkansas limestone: calcium and carbonate and almost nothing else. Chloride is 1.1 ppm, sulfate 5.2, sodium below the reporting limit entirely — so of the six ions, four are effectively absent and the water is very nearly pure calcium bicarbonate. Residual alkalinity around 58. That makes it an unusually clean canvas for a malty beer: the carbonate is already there for dark malt, and you set the flavour ions yourself from zero.

waterProfiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Salem, SC)
waterProfiles.description: The softest water in this entire table that is not distilled. Every ion is in single figures and alkalinity is 22 ppm as CaCO3, giving a residual alkalinity near 16 — genuinely close to a blank slate, and the best off-the-shelf starting point here for a pale, delicate lager. Unlike the blended brands, it is a single named spring, so the figure is a figure rather than a range.

waterProfiles.name: Crystal Geyser (Olancha Peak, CA)
waterProfiles.description: Eastern Sierra snowmelt, soft and low in everything except sodium, which runs 15 to 18 ppm — enough to round the palate without tasting of anything. The one figure that moves is sulfate, which the report gives as 8.5 to 25 ppm; at the top of that range it will noticeably sharpen hop bitterness and at the bottom it will not, so treat the hop character as the variable and everything else as settled.

waterProfiles.name: Saratoga Spring Water
waterProfiles.description: Blended from several springs like the big brands, but the range barely matters: calcium stays between 7.5 and 9 ppm and alkalinity between 9.7 and 28 as CaCO3, so every bottle is soft and nearly free of carbonate whichever spring it came from. Residual alkalinity is around 13 at the midpoint. Along with Ozarka and the Salem spring, this is one of the few American waters you can treat as a near-blank slate without testing it first.

additives.name: Tartaric Acid
additives.description: The principal grape acid and the only common wine acid that resists metabolism by lactic bacteria. Adding 1 g/L raises titratable acidity by about 1 g/L and lowers pH, though how far depends on the must's buffering.
additives.usageNotes: The default acidulant for grape wine. Add before fermentation so the potassium bitartrate has time to precipitate out during cold stabilisation.
additives.cautions: Some of what you add will drop out as tartrate crystals, so the measured TA after cold stabilisation will be lower than the arithmetic predicts.
additives.attribution: Acid and deacidification figures are the standard oenological approximations: 1 g/L of a monoprotic addition moves titratable acidity by roughly 1 g/L, expressed as tartaric. Real musts are buffered, so the pH change for a given TA change varies with potassium and the starting acid profile — always measure rather than assuming. Compiled from OIV oenological practice and standard winemaking references.

additives.name: Malic Acid
additives.description: The sharp green-apple acid of apples, stone fruit and unripe grapes. Tastes harsher than tartaric at the same titratable acidity.
additives.usageNotes: The natural acid of cider and most fruit. Use where a crisp, appley acidity is wanted.
additives.cautions: Lactic bacteria convert malic to lactic acid, softening the wine and releasing CO2 — a bottled wine with residual malic can referment.
additives.attribution: Acid and deacidification figures are the standard oenological approximations: 1 g/L of a monoprotic addition moves titratable acidity by roughly 1 g/L, expressed as tartaric. Real musts are buffered, so the pH change for a given TA change varies with potassium and the starting acid profile — always measure rather than assuming. additives.usageNotes: Common in fruit wines and meads, where its flavour fits. Also chelates iron and copper.
additives.cautions: Lactic bacteria metabolise citric acid to diacetyl and acetic acid — do not use it in a wine that will undergo malolactic conversion.

additives.name: Potassium Bicarbonate
additives.description: The standard wine deacidifier: roughly 1 g/L drops titratable acidity by about 1 g/L, precipitating the acid as potassium bitartrate.

additives.cautions: Do not exceed about 3 g/L — beyond that the wine turns salty and flat, and the pH rise brings microbial risk. Effect only completes after cold stabilisation.

additives.name: Potassium Metabisulfite
additives.description: The workhorse antimicrobial and antioxidant of winemaking. About 57.6% SO2 by weight, so 1 g/L yields roughly 576 mg/L SO2 — in practice dosed in tens of milligrams per litre.
additives.usageNotes: What matters is not free SO2 but molecular SO2, which is pH-dependent: molecular = free / (1 + 10^(pH - 1.81)). Target around 0.5-0.8 mg/L molecular. At pH 3.2 that needs roughly 20 mg/L free; at pH 3.8 it needs over 80.
additives.cautions: Legal total-SO2 limits apply — 350 mg/L in the US for table wine, lower in the EU and lower again for organic. Some people are genuinely sulphite-sensitive; declaration is mandatory above 10 mg/L in most markets.
additives.attribution: Sulphite chemistry follows the standard molecular SO2 relationship, molecular = free / (1 + 10^(pH - 1.81)), where 1.81 is the first pKa of sulphurous acid. Legal total-SO2 and sorbate limits differ by jurisdiction and by product category — the figures cited are US TTB values for table wine and are not universal. Check your own regulator.

Extraction rate depends on format, toast, temperature and alcohol — the ranges here are starting points for a tasting schedule, not endpoints.

additives.name: Mizunara Oak
additives.description: Japanese oak, prized for a sandalwood, coconut and incense character that develops only over long maturation.
additives.usageNotes: The signature of Japanese whisky finishing.
additives.cautions: Notoriously porous and leaky as a barrel wood, and expensive. The character takes many years to emerge.
additives.attribution: Wood dose rates assume chips or cubes in a homebrew-scale vessel and are far higher per litre than a barrel's surface-to-volume ratio would give. Extraction rate depends on format, toast, temperature and alcohol — the ranges here are starting points for a tasting schedule, not endpoints.

legalStandards.title: Africa: Indigenous Grain Beers, Honey Wine & Palm Wine
legalStandards.attribution: Africa's indigenous ferments — sorghum and millet opaque beers, Ethiopian honey wine, palm wine — predate and stand apart from European brewing traditions. Most have no statutory definition; a few (Ethiopian tej, industrial sorghum beer) are commercially produced. Documented from ethnographic and food-science sources; values are typical.

styles.name: Umqombothi / Sorghum Beer
styles.impression: Southern Africa's traditional beer: thick, sour, opaque and still actively fermenting when drunk — pinkish-brown, gritty, and sipped from a shared clay pot.
styles.comments: Central to Xhosa and Zulu ritual — weddings, funerals, ancestral ceremonies. The lactic sourness and low alcohol are defining; it is as much food as drink. Industrially produced as 'Chibuku' shake-shake in cartons.
styles.ingredients: Maize meal and sorghum malt, soured by lactic fermentation then alcohol-fermented by wild yeast. Left unfiltered and drunk live.

styles.name: Pito / Burukutu / Dolo
styles.impression: West Africa's sorghum and millet beers — cloudy, tart and dark, brewed by (usually women) and sold fresh at markets.
styles.comments: Pito (Ghana, Nigeria), dolo (Burkina Faso), burukutu (Nigeria). Drunk warm and fresh from calabashes within a day or two.
styles.ingredients: Malted sorghum or millet, mashed, soured and fermented with wild yeast and a pitched portion of a previous brew.
styles.tags: africa, sorghum, millet, pito, dolo, traditional

styles.name: Tella / Injera-Grain Beer (ጠላ)
styles.impression: Ethiopia's homebrewed grain beer — smoky, tart and dark, flavoured with gesho (buckthorn) as the bittering agent in place of hops.
styles.comments: Gesho is Africa's closest analogue to hops — a bittering, preserving plant. Tella is the everyday house beer; a stronger, filtered version exists for guests.
styles.ingredients: Roasted barley, wheat or other grain with gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) leaves and twigs, fermented in a clay pot; the vessel is often smoked with olivewood.

styles.name: Tej / Berz (ጠጅ)
styles.impression: Ethiopian and Eritrean honey wine — sweet, cloudy, deceptively strong, and bittered with gesho. The ancestral drink of the Ethiopian court.
styles.comments: Served in a rounded flask (berele). Strength varies wildly with fermentation time and honey ratio. A defining feature is the gesho bittering, which links it to tella.
styles.ingredients: Honey and water fermented with wild yeast, bittered with gesho (Rhamnus prinoides). Berz is the young, near-non-alcoholic stage.

styles.name: Palm Wine (Emu / Nsafufuo / Matango)
styles.impression: Tapped palm sap that ferments spontaneously into a sweet, effervescent, milky wine within hours — sweeter fresh, sourer and stronger as the day goes on.
styles.comments: Drunk across West and Central Africa (and the tropics worldwide). Central to ceremony — marriage, naming, libation. Distilled it becomes ogogoro / akpeteshie.
styles.ingredients: Sap of oil, raffia or coconut palms, collected from the felled or standing tree; wild yeast ferments it immediately.

styles.name: Akpeteshie / Ogogoro (Distilled Palm Spirit)
styles.impression: West Africa's distilled palm spirit — fiery, raw and potent, long outlawed under colonial rule and now a proud local spirit.
styles.comments: Akpeteshie (Ghana), ogogoro (Nigeria). Banned by colonial authorities protecting imported liquor; became a symbol of independence.
styles.ingredients: Fermented palm wine, pot-distilled.

legalStandards.title: Beer: Legal Definitions, Purity Laws & Protected Designations
legalStandards.attribution: Competition style guidelines describe how a beer should taste. Beer *law* describes what may legally be called beer, and in some places dictates the recipe outright. This edition compiles binding legal texts rather than sensory targets: Germany's Vorläufiges Biergesetz (the modern Reinheitsgebot), the Kölsch Konvention, EU PDO/PGI/TSG registrations (Münchner Bier, Bayerisches Bier, České pivo, Oude Geuze, Kriek), Belgian royal decrees on lambic, US 26 U.S.C. §5052 and 27 CFR Parts 7 and 25, Japan's Liquor Tax Act as amended in 2018, Brazil's Decreto 6.871 and Mexico's NOM-199-SCFI. Numeric ranges are legal minima/maxima or the gravity bands used for taxation — not judging ranges — so a beer can be legal and still taste nothing like the archetype. Always check the current instrument for the jurisdiction you brew in; these are summaries, not legal advice.

styles.name: Reinheitsgebot (Bavarian Purity Law, 1516)
styles.impression: The historical ancestor of every purity law: beer may contain only barley, hops and water.
styles.ingredients: Barley (Gerste), hops (Hopfen), water (Wasser). Yeast is absent from the text — Pasteur's work was three and a half centuries away, and fermentation was understood as spontaneous.
styles.comments: Promulgated by Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria at Ingolstadt on 23 April 1516, primarily as a price-fixing and food-security measure: restricting brewers to barley reserved wheat and rye for bread. It also capped the price of beer by the Mass. It applied only to Bavaria; the rest of what became Germany brewed with gruit, wheat, oats, spices and fruit for centuries afterwards. Wheat beer survived in Bavaria only as a ducal monopoly licensed outside the law.
styles.history: Extended nationally as a condition of Bavaria joining the German Empire in 1871 and the Weimar Republic in 1919; struck down as a trade barrier for imports by the European Court of Justice in 1987 (Case 178/84), which held Germany could not bar lawfully-produced beer from other member states. Domestic German brewers remained bound by the successor statute.
styles.examples: Cited on the label of most German breweries as a marketing claim ("gebraut nach dem Reinheitsgebot") rather than as the operative law, which is the 1993 statute below.

styles.name: Vorläufiges Biergesetz — Bottom-Fermented Beer
styles.impression: The operative modern German purity law for lagers: malted grain, hops, yeast, water. Nothing else.
styles.ingredients: Malted barley (or other malted grain), hops, yeast and water only. Hop products (extract, pellets, isomerised extract) and technical processing aids that are removed are permitted; unmalted adjuncts and sugar are not.
styles.comments: Vorläufiges Biergesetz of 29 July 1993, §9(1). Because the statute reaches only bottom-fermented beer here, a German lager cannot legally contain rice, maize, sugar or unmalted barley for the domestic market. Filtration aids, water treatment salts, and gases are governed separately and do not count as ingredients.
styles.history: Succeeded the 1906 Biersteuergesetz, itself the national extension of the Bavarian 1516 order. The 'vorläufig' (provisional) in the title has outlived thirty years of provisionality.
styles.examples: Every domestically-sold German Pils, Helles, Märzen, Bock, Schwarzbier

styles.name: Vorläufiges Biergesetz — Top-Fermented Beer
styles.impression: The looser branch of the German purity law, which is why Weissbier, Kölsch and Berliner Weisse are lawful.
styles.ingredients: Malted grain of any kind (barley, wheat, rye, spelt, oats), hops, yeast, water — plus technically pure cane, beet or invert sugar, glucose, and colourings derived from those sugars.
styles.comments: Vorläufiges Biergesetz §9(2). The sugar allowance for top-fermented beer is what permits candi-style sugars and the colour adjustment used in some dark wheat beers. Unmalted grain remains prohibited, so a German-brewed witbier with raw wheat cannot be sold domestically as 'Bier' without the special permit below.
styles.history: The distinction dates to the 1906 imperial law, which took a pragmatic view of the northern German top-fermenting tradition that Bavaria's order had never covered.
styles.examples: Weissbier, Kölsch, Altbier, Berliner Weisse, Gose (by special permit)

styles.name: Besondere Biere (§9(7) Special Permit)
styles.impression: The escape hatch: a case-by-case exemption allowing beers that would otherwise breach the purity law.
styles.ingredients: Whatever the granting state authority approves — historically fruit, spices, salt, coriander, herbs, and unmalted grain.
styles.comments: Vorläufiges Biergesetz §9(7)–(8) lets the competent Land authority permit 'besondere Biere' (special beers) and beers brewed for export or experiment. This is the legal basis on which Leipziger Gose and Berliner Weisse with additions, and the modern German craft sector's fruited and spiced beers, are produced. Beers made for export need not comply at all — German breweries routinely brew adjunct lagers for foreign markets.
styles.history: Formalised the ad-hoc dispensations that had kept Gose and other regional oddities alive through the 20th century.
styles.examples: Leipziger Gose, German-brewed craft fruit and spice beers

styles.name: German Beer Tax Classes by Stammwürze
styles.impression: Not a style, but the gravity bands that decide German beer tax — and the reason 'Bock' means a number, not a flavour.
styles.comments: Biersteuergesetz bands by original gravity (Stammwürze, °P): Einfachbier 2.0–5.5 °P; Schankbier 7.0–11.0 °P; Vollbier 11.0–16.0 °P; Starkbier (which includes every legal Bock and Doppelbock) 16.0 °P and above. The 5.5–7.0 °P gap is a genuine discontinuity in the statute. Tax is assessed per hectolitre per degree Plato. This is why a German brewer calling a beer 'Bock' is making a claim about gravity that carries legal weight, unlike an American brewer using the same word.
styles.history: The Plato-based structure dates to the 19th-century Bavarian Malzaufschlag (malt levy) and survived the shift to a finished-beer excise.
styles.ingredients: 1.008–1.085 in the OG columns is the approximate specific-gravity span of the bands (2 °P to ~20 °P), given for calculator convenience only.

styles.name: Kölsch (Kölsch-Konvention & PGI)
styles.impression: A pale, bright, hop-accented, top-fermented Vollbier — legally definable only if brewed in and around Cologne.
styles.ingredients: Compliant with the Vorläufiges Biergesetz top-fermented rules; in practice Pilsner malt, sometimes a small wheat portion, German hops, and a top-fermenting yeast fermented cool and lagered.
styles.comments: The Kölsch-Konvention of 6 March 1986 is a private agreement among Cologne brewers, given teeth by registration as a Protected Geographical Indication in 1997. It requires the beer to be top-fermented, pale, filtered bright (blank), hop-accentuated, of Vollbier strength, and brewed within the defined Cologne region. Serving in the 0.2 L Stange is convention, not law. A beer brewed elsewhere may be described as 'Kölsch-style' but may not be sold as Kölsch in the EU/UK.
styles.history: The Konvention was drafted to stop the name being used by brewers outside the city after Kölsch's post-war revival; it named an initial closed list of signatory breweries.

styles.name: Münchner Bier & Bayerisches Bier (PGI)
styles.impression: Geography as an ingredient: these names attach to place of brewing, not to a recipe.
styles.ingredients: Purity-law compliant; Münchner Bier additionally requires brewing water drawn from Munich's own deep wells within the city boundary.
styles.comments: Münchner Bier was registered as a Protected Geographical Indication in 1998 and covers the full range brewed by the qualifying Munich breweries — Helles, Hell Export, Weissbier, Märzen/Oktoberfestbier, Dunkel, Bock and Doppelbock — so long as the entire brewing process takes place in Munich. Bayerisches Bier (PGI, 2001) is the wider Bavarian equivalent. Related registrations include Bremer Bier, Dortmunder Bier, Kulmbacher Bier, Hofer Bier and Mainfranken Bier. Only the six Munich breweries within the boundary may pour at Oktoberfest.
styles.history: Registered under what is now Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs.
styles.examples: Augustiner, Hacker-Pschorr, Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Paulaner, Spaten

styles.name: České pivo (Czech Beer, PGI)
styles.impression: The only major protected designation that prescribes not just place and ingredients but analytical outcomes — including a permitted diacetyl level.
styles.ingredients: Czech-grown barley malt of listed varieties, Czech hop varieties from the Žatec, Úštěk and Tršice regions (Saaz and its descendants), Czech brewing water, and bottom-fermenting yeast. Decoction mashing and open or traditional fermentation are part of the specification.
styles.comments: Registered as a Protected Geographical Indication in 2008 after a long negotiation with the European Commission. The specification is unusually quantitative: it fixes ranges for original gravity, apparent attenuation (notably *lower* than international lagers, leaving residual sweetness), bitterness, colour, polyphenol content and pH, and it permits a measurable diacetyl concentration that most brewing traditions would treat as a defect. The ranges above span the covered light and dark sub-types rather than describing one beer.
styles.history: Sought after EU accession to protect the domestic character of Czech lager against pressure to converge on international adjunct lager.
styles.examples: Pilsner Urquell, Budvar, Kozel, Bernard, Svijany

styles.name: Czech Gravity Classes (Výčepní / Ležák / Speciál)
styles.impression: The Czech shorthand every pub uses: beers are named by their degrees, not their style.
styles.comments: Czech regulation classifies beer by original gravity in degrees Plato: lehké (light) under 8 °P; výčepní (draught/tap) 8–10 °P; ležák (lager) 11–12 °P; speciál 13 °P and above; plus porter at 18 °P or more. The familiar '10°' and '12°' on a Czech tap handle are these classes, not ABV. A '12' is the flagship pale lager of most breweries; a '10' is the everyday session beer. The class is a labelling requirement, so it is legally meaningful in a way that the English word 'lager' is not.
styles.history: Carries over from the Austro-Hungarian gravity-based malt taxation that also shaped the German bands.
styles.ingredients: No ingredient restriction attaches to the class itself; České pivo PGI status is separate.

styles.name: Žatecký chmel (Saaz Hops, PDO)
styles.impression: An ingredient with its own protected designation — the reason 'Saaz' on a hop packet is a claim about a valley, not a plant.
styles.ingredients: Hops of the Saaz (Žatecký poloraný červeňák) landrace grown in the delimited Žatec hop-growing region of north-west Bohemia.
styles.comments: Registered as a Protected Designation of Origin. Hops of the same genetic variety grown in the United States are lawfully sold as 'Saaz' or 'US Saaz' outside the EU but cannot carry the protected Czech designation, and analytically differ — usually higher alpha and cohumulone, different oil profile. Brewers substituting one for the other should expect a perceptible difference, which is why the substitution tables in this site treat them as related but distinct.
styles.history: The Žatec growing region's reputation predates the modern designation by several centuries; sealing and provenance marks were used from the 1880s.
styles.examples: Saaz used in Pilsner Urquell, Budvar

styles.name: Authentic Trappist Product
styles.impression: Not a style at all — a certification about who brews, where, and what happens to the money.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted. The Trappist designation says nothing about recipe; certified breweries make everything from 4.8% table beer to 12% quadrupels, and the label also covers cheese, bread and cosmetics.
styles.comments: The hexagonal Authentic Trappist Product logo is awarded by the International Trappist Association on three criteria: the beer is brewed within the walls of a Trappist abbey; production is carried out by or under the supervision of the monastic community; and the proceeds are directed to the community's needs and to social work, not to shareholder profit. Certification is withdrawn when a monastery ceases to meet them — as has happened more than once — so the roster changes over time and any list should be checked against the ITA's current one.
styles.history: The mark was introduced in 1997 after commercial brewers began using 'Trappist' as a descriptor; a Belgian court had earlier found the term protectable.
styles.examples: Historically Westmalle, Westvleteren, Rochefort, Orval, Chimay, Achel, La Trappe, Zundert, Tre Fontane, Spencer, Tynt Meadow, Mont des Cats and others — the certified list is not static

styles.name: Certified Belgian Abbey Beer
styles.impression: The commercial tier below Trappist: a real monastic link, but the beer is brewed by a business.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted.
styles.comments: Administered by the Belgian Brewers federation. Requires a genuine link to an existing or historical abbey — a licence from the monastic body, or a documented historical connection — with the abbey retaining a say in marketing and receiving royalties that support it or its charitable works. It does not require monastic supervision of brewing, and the beer may be contract-brewed. 'Abbey-style' beers with no such link may use the flavour descriptor but not the certification mark.
styles.history: Created in 1999 to give commercial abbey brands a defensible standard after the Trappist mark closed off the stronger claim.
styles.examples: Leffe, Grimbergen, Affligem, Maredsous, St. Bernardus

styles.name: Lambic (Belgian Royal Decree)
styles.impression: The rare case where spontaneous fermentation is written into statute.
styles.ingredients: At least 30% unmalted wheat alongside barley malt; aged hops used for their preservative effect rather than bitterness; no cultured yeast pitched — fermentation proceeds from the ambient microflora.
styles.comments: Belgian royal decree (1965, revised 1993) defines lambic as a spontaneously-fermented beer produced by the traditional method, sets the minimum unmalted wheat proportion at 30%, and requires maturation in wood. Measured IBU is near meaningless: aged hops contribute little isomerised bitterness, so the figures above reflect analysis rather than perceived bitterness, and the acidity comes from Brettanomyces, Pediococcus and Lactobacillus rather than from hops.
styles.history: Codified a Pajottenland and Zenne valley practice already centuries old; the decree was a defensive measure as sweetened and blended commercial products spread.
styles.examples: Cantillon, Boon, Girardin, Lindemans, De Troch (unblended lambic is rarely bottled)
styles.tags: belgium, spontaneous, wheat, wood-aged, sour, statute

styles.name: Oude Geuze & Oude Kriek (TSG)
styles.impression: Blended, bottle-refermented lambic — protected as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed, where the word 'Oude' is the operative legal term.
styles.ingredients: Lambic only, of differing ages, blended; for Oude Kriek, sour cherries macerated in lambic. No sweetening, no artificial colour or flavour, no post-blend pasteurisation.
styles.comments: Registered as Traditional Specialities Guaranteed in 1997 for Gueuze/Geuze, Oude Geuze, Kriek and Oude Kriek. The specification requires a blend of lambics including a proportion of at least three years old, refermented in the bottle, and — critically — reserves 'Oude'/'Vieille' for the unsweetened traditional product. A bottle labelled simply 'Geuze' or 'Kriek' without 'Oude' may be sweetened, filtered and pasteurised, which is why the adjective is the single most useful word on a Belgian sour label. The HORAL producers' association applies further criteria to its members.
styles.history: The TSG scheme protects a method rather than a place, which suits a product defined by blending and ageing practice.
styles.examples: Oude Geuze Boon, 3 Fonteinen Oude Geuze, Cantillon Kriek
styles.tags: belgium, TSG, blended, bottle-conditioned, sour, protected-name

styles.name: UK 'Beer' for Duty Purposes
styles.impression: No purity law, no recipe rules — Britain regulates beer almost entirely through alcoholic strength and tax.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted. Sugar, maize, torrefied wheat, flaked barley and brewing syrups have been normal British practice since the mid-19th century, when the malt tax gave way to a beer duty and invert sugar became lawful.
styles.comments: Under the Alcoholic Liquor Duties Act 1979, and now the Alcohol Duty regime introduced in August 2023, beer is charged by strength: products at or below 1.2% ABV fall outside alcohol duty entirely, with banded rates above that and Draught Relief for qualifying containers of 20 litres or more. Small Producer Relief replaced Small Brewers Relief. There is no ingredient restriction and no protected recipe — 'IPA', 'stout' and 'bitter' carry no legal meaning in the UK.
styles.history: The Free Mash-Tun Act of 1880 abolished the malt tax and shifted duty to the wort's gravity, legalising sugar and adjuncts and shaping British brewing for a century.

styles.name: Real Ale (CAMRA Definition)
styles.impression: A private definition with more cultural force than most statutes: beer that finishes fermenting in the vessel it is served from.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted, though finings (traditionally isinglass) are conventional; unfined and vegan-friendly cask beer is now common.
styles.comments: The Campaign for Real Ale defines real ale as beer brewed from traditional ingredients, matured by secondary fermentation in the container from which it is dispensed, and served without the use of extraneous carbon dioxide. Cask breathers — which blanket the beer with CO2 at atmospheric pressure to exclude oxygen — were long excluded and are now accepted by CAMRA. 'Real ale in a bottle' is the bottle-conditioned equivalent. None of this is law: it is a consumer organisation's standard that the trade adopted.
styles.history: CAMRA was founded in 1971 in reaction to keg bitter and national brewery consolidation; the definition is the campaign's central instrument.
styles.examples: Cask-conditioned bitter, mild, porter served by handpump or gravity

styles.name: Irish Beer Excise & Descriptive Practice
styles.impression: Like Britain: strength-based duty, no compositional rules, and a national style protected only by reputation.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted. Irish stout's characteristic grist — pale malt, flaked barley and roasted unmalted barley — is convention, not requirement, and the roasted barley portion is what distinguishes it from an English stout built on black malt.
styles.comments: Beer duty is charged by Revenue on alcohol content, with a relief scheme for small independent producers. There is no PGI for Irish stout or Irish red ale; 'Irish Whiskey' by contrast is tightly protected by a technical file (see the Spirits edition). A brewer anywhere in the world may lawfully label a beer 'Irish stout'.
styles.history: Ireland's excise structure descends from the same 19th-century UK gravity-based system, diverging after independence.

styles.name: Beer (26 U.S.C. §5052 / 27 CFR 25.11)
styles.impression: The federal tax definition: fermented from malt, or from a malt substitute, with hops, at half a percent or more.
styles.ingredients: Malt, or a substitute for malt, plus hops or hop products, water and yeast. 27 CFR 25.15 permits a broad range of adjuncts and processing materials.
styles.comments: For excise purposes beer is 'beer, ale, porter, stout, and other similar fermented beverages of any name or description containing one-half of one percent or more of alcohol by volume, brewed or produced from malt, wholly or in part, or from any substitute therefor.' A beer that contains no malted barley, or no hops — a sorghum ale, a gruit — falls outside the TTB's labelling authority under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act and is regulated by the FDA instead, which is why some gluten-free and unhopped products carry FDA nutrition labels. Federal law does not cap beer ABV, but several states do, and state definitions of 'beer' frequently diverge from the federal one.
styles.history: The 0.5% threshold is a direct survival of the Volstead Act's definition of an intoxicating beverage.

styles.name: Malt Beverage Labelling (27 CFR Part 7)
styles.impression: What a US label may and may not say — the closest thing America has to a style rulebook, and it barely mentions styles.
styles.ingredients: Not prescribed; the rules govern statements, not composition.
styles.comments: Part 7 requires a Certificate of Label Approval for most malt beverages, governs brand names and geographic claims, restricts health-related statements, and controls strength statements. Geographic terms that have become generic in the US — 'pilsner', 'india pale ale' — may be used freely; terms recognised as distinctive to a place may not be used misleadingly. There is no federal definition of 'IPA', 'craft', or 'session'. The Alcohol Facts / Serving Facts statement is optional but increasingly used. The Brewers Association's 'independent craft' seal is a trade-association mark with no legal force.
styles.history: Enacted under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act of 1935 as part of the post-Prohibition regulatory settlement.

styles.name: Japan — 'Beer' (Liquor Tax Act, as amended 2018)
styles.impression: A malt-percentage definition, loosened in 2018 — the change that made Japanese craft beer with fruit and spices legally 'beer'.
styles.ingredients: Malt exceeding 50% of the grist (lowered from the previous 67%), water and hops as principal ingredients, with permitted secondary ingredients — historically rice, maize, sorghum, potato, starch and sugar, extended in 2018 to fruit, spices, herbs and flowers — capped at 5% of the weight of the malt.
styles.comments: Before April 2018 a Japanese beer flavoured with orange peel or coriander was legally happōshu and taxed differently; the reform brought such beers into the 'beer' class and is the single most consequential legal change for Japanese craft brewing. The two-thirds malt threshold had also driven the industry to invent low-malt categories purely for tax reasons.
styles.history: The 1994 reduction of the minimum annual production volume for a brewing licence from 2,000 kL to 60 kL created the ji-biru (local beer) sector; the 2018 ingredient reform completed the opening.
styles.examples: Japanese-brewed pale lager, and post-2018 fruited and spiced craft beer

styles.name: Japan — Happōshu & 'New Genre' (Third Beer)
styles.impression: Two entire product categories that exist for no reason other than tax arbitrage.
styles.ingredients: Happōshu: malt below the 'beer' threshold, or beer-like beverages using ingredients outside the permitted list. New genre: either no malt at all — pea protein, soy peptide and other bases — or happōshu blended with a distilled spirit.
styles.comments: Because Japanese excise was assessed by malt content, brewers engineered products just below each threshold. Happōshu (sparkling liquor) came first in the 1990s; 'third beer' or new genre followed when happōshu itself was taxed up. Japan is now unifying the rates for beer, happōshu and new genre in staged steps, which removes the incentive and is expected to shrink the low-malt categories.
styles.history: Suntory's Hop's (1994) is generally credited as the first modern happōshu.
styles.examples: Kirin Tanrei, Asahi Style Free, Suntory Kinmugi, Sapporo Mugi to Hop

styles.name: Brazil — Cerveja (Decreto 6.871/2009)
styles.impression: A malt-majority rule with a generous adjunct allowance — written for a market built on maize and rice.
styles.ingredients: Barley malt must constitute at least 55% of the extract; up to 45% may come from unmalted cereals (maize, rice, wheat, sorghum) and sugars. Hops or hop products, water, yeast.
styles.comments: Decreto nº 6.871/2009 implementing Lei 8.918/1994 sets the classification of beer by extract, colour and fermentation type, and requires labelling of the beer's classification. Beers using more than the permitted adjunct proportion must be labelled and sold under a different designation. The 2019 Belo Horizonte methanol-free contamination episodes prompted tighter supervision of brewery quality controls.
styles.history: Brazil's classification system predates its craft boom and has been repeatedly amended to accommodate it.
styles.examples: Brazilian-brewed pilsen, and the growing craft sector

styles.name: Mexico — Cerveza (NOM-199-SCFI)
styles.impression: A national standard covering composition, labelling and the alcohol range a product may claim.
styles.ingredients: Malted cereals — barley malt principally — with permitted adjuncts including maize and rice, hops or hop extracts, water and yeast.
styles.comments: NOM-199-SCFI-2017 sets out the specifications and test methods for alcoholic beverages including beer, covering denomination, alcohol content declaration, and labelling. The Mexican adjunct lager tradition, built on maize, is the product of a market shaped by Central European immigrant brewers working with local grain rather than of any legal constraint.
styles.history: Mexican brewing carries a strong Austro-Bavarian inheritance from the 19th-century Habsburg period and later German immigration, adapted to maize.
styles.examples: Mexican-brewed lager and the domestic craft sector

styles.name: Gluten-Free Beer (Codex / FDA / EU 20 ppm)
styles.impression: A claim with a hard number behind it — and a regulatory split over enzyme-treated barley beer that matters to coeliac drinkers.
styles.ingredients: Either naturally gluten-free bases (sorghum, millet, rice, buckwheat, maize) or barley beer treated with a prolyl endopeptidase to hydrolyse gluten peptides.
styles.comments: Codex Alimentarius, EU Regulation 828/2014 and the US FDA all set 20 mg/kg (20 ppm) as the ceiling for a gluten-free claim. The dispute is over measurement: the standard R5 ELISA does not reliably quantify the *fragments* left by enzyme treatment, so a treated barley beer may test below 20 ppm while still containing immunoreactive peptides. The FDA therefore does not permit an unqualified 'gluten-free' claim for beers made from gluten-containing grain and treated to remove it; such beers are labelled 'crafted to remove gluten' in the US, while the EU and Australia have taken different positions. Homebrewers should not treat an enzyme-treated beer as safe for a coeliac drinker.
styles.history: Clarilex/Brewers Clarex-type enzymes were adopted for haze reduction; the gluten-reduction effect was a by-product that outran the analytical methods.
styles.examples: Sorghum-based gluten-free beers; 'crafted to remove gluten' barley beers

styles.name: Non-Alcoholic & Low-Alcohol Thresholds
styles.impression: The same bottle can be 'non-alcoholic' in one country and 'low-alcohol' in the next.
styles.ingredients: Unrestricted; produced by arrested fermentation, vacuum distillation, reverse osmosis, or maltose-negative yeasts such as Saccharomycodes ludwigii.
styles.comments: The US permits 'non-alcoholic' for malt beverages below 0.5% ABV but reserves 'alcohol-free' for 0.0%; the UK's guidance sets alcohol-free at 0.05% or below, de-alcoholised at 0.5% or below, and low-alcohol at 1.2% or below; Germany allows 'alkoholfrei' up to 0.5%; Spain and several other EU states use 1.0%. Because ordinary bread, kombucha and fruit juice can exceed 0.5%, the thresholds are pragmatic rather than absolute. Brewers should note that residual fermentables in a de-alcoholised beer make it microbiologically fragile and usually require pasteurisation or sterile filtration.
styles.history: The category was a Prohibition-era survival before its modern commercial revival.
styles.examples: Athletic Brewing, Erdinger Alkoholfrei, Guinness 0.0, Lucky Saint

styles.name: Organic Beer (NOP / EU 2018/848)
styles.impression: A supply-chain certification rather than a recipe rule — and hops are the usual sticking point.
styles.ingredients: Certified organic malt, hops and adjuncts; permitted processing aids only.
styles.comments: Under the USDA National Organic Program, '100% organic' requires all ingredients certified; 'organic' requires at least 95% by weight, with the remainder from the National List; 'made with organic ingredients' requires at least 70%. EU Regulation 2018/848 operates comparably. Organic hops were on the US National List as a permitted non-organic exception until 2013, after which organic beer required organic hops — a change that materially constrained the category, since organic hop acreage is small and variety choice limited.
styles.history: The 2013 removal of the hop exception is the defining event in US organic brewing.
styles.examples: Certified organic beers under NOP or EU marks

legalStandards.title: Mongolia & Central Asia: Milk Ferments and Their Spirits
legalStandards.attribution: The steppe's defining drinks are fermented from mare's and other animal milk — a lineage unique among the world's alcohols. Documented from ethnographic and dairy-science sources; there is no judging guideline for any of them. Values are typical.

styles.name: Airag / Kumis (айраг / кумыс)
styles.impression: Fermented mare's milk — the national drink of Mongolia and the Central Asian steppe. Sour, fizzy, faintly alcoholic and thin, with a sharp dairy tang.
styles.comments: Both lactic-acid bacteria and yeast work at once, so it is simultaneously soured and lightly alcoholic. A pillar of nomadic nutrition; drunk in large quantities in summer. Kumis is the Turkic/Kazakh name, airag the Mongolian.
styles.ingredients: Raw mare's milk, fermented by a mixed lactic-and-yeast culture in a leather bag (khokhuur) or vat, churned thousands of times to aerate. Mare's milk is uniquely high in the lactose the yeast ferment.

styles.name: Tarasun / Milk-Whey Beers
styles.impression: Regional cow- or yak-milk ferments of Buryatia and the wider steppe, sometimes stronger than airag.
styles.comments: Where mares are scarce, other animals' milk is fermented similarly. Shubat (camel) is prized in Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.
