styles.comments: Conventional practice passes pressed sake over activated charcoal to remove colour and soften rough aromatics. Muroka omits it, leaving a faintly golden or greenish tint and a fuller, more assertive flavour. Frequently combined as muroka nama genshu — unfiltered, unpasteurised, undiluted — which is about as unmediated as commercial sake gets and is a hallmark of the modern jizake movement.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Charcoal filtration became standard in the 20th century for cosmetic consistency; muroka is a deliberate reversal.

styles.name: Koshu / Jukusei-shu (古酒・熟成酒) — Aged Sake
styles.impression: Deliberately matured — amber to brown, with sherry, mushroom, caramel and soy notes.
styles.comments: There is no statutory minimum age for the term, though the Long-Term Aged Sake Producers Association applies a three-year convention for jukusei koshu. Ageing drives Maillard chemistry between amino acids and sugars, darkening the sake and building umami; warm-aged examples develop quickly and heavily, cold-aged ones more slowly and delicately. Junmai and kijōshu age best because they carry the amino acid load to work with. Sake is otherwise conventionally treated as a fresh product with a stated brewing year (BY) rather than a vintage.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Aged sake was recorded in the Edo period, disappeared under the Meiji tax regime that charged duty at production, and returned from the 1970s.

styles.name: Sparkling Sake / Awasake (スパークリング清酒)
styles.impression: Carbonated sake, from lightly petillant nigori to bottle-fermented and disgorged.
styles.comments: Not a tax-law designation. The awasake Association applies a voluntary standard for the premium end: bottle-refermented, no added carbon dioxide, clear after disgorgement or fine filtration, minimum pressure, and made only from rice, koji and water. Below that sits a large market of low-alcohol force-carbonated products around 5–8% ABV. Bottle-conditioned nigori sits in between and is often actively fermenting in the bottle.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade; secondary fermentation from residual or added sugar.
styles.history: The premium bottle-fermented category dates to the 2010s and the awasake standard to 2016.
styles.examples: Bottle-fermented awasake and commodity sparkling sake

styles.name: GI Nihonshu (日本酒) — 'Japanese Sake'
styles.impression: A national geographical indication: only sake made in Japan from Japanese rice may be called nihonshu.
styles.ingredients: Rice grown in Japan, rice koji made from Japanese rice, and water; the entire production — fermentation, pressing, filtration and bottling — carried out in Japan.
styles.comments: Designated by the National Tax Agency in December 2015. Sake brewed outside Japan, of which there is now a substantial quantity in the United States, Canada, France, Norway and elsewhere, remains legally seishu-equivalent in its own jurisdiction but cannot be labelled nihonshu for markets recognising the GI. The designation protects the word, not the method — a foreign brewer may use identical rice varieties, koji and technique.
styles.history: Part of a broader Japanese push to secure GI protection for its agricultural and beverage exports.
styles.examples: All Japan-produced sake meeting the conditions

styles.name: Regional Sake GIs (Yamagata, Hakusan, Nada, Harima…)
styles.impression: Prefectural and sub-regional designations, each with its own production specification and tasting panel.
styles.ingredients: Set by each individual GI specification — typically prescribing local water, permitted rice, production within the delimited area, and a sensory approval step.
styles.comments: GI Hakusan (Ishikawa, 2005) was the first, followed by GI Yamagata (2016) — the first covering an entire prefecture — and subsequently Nada Gogo (Hyogo), Harima, Mie, Nagano, Toyama, Saga, Yamanashi and others. Specifications commonly require that the rice and water be local, that the sake be brewed and bottled within the area, and that it pass an organoleptic assessment before the designation may be used. Because each is distinct, the GI on a label tells you the sake met a regional committee's standard, not that it belongs to a defined flavour category.
styles.history: Modelled on European wine appellation practice and administered by the National Tax Agency.
styles.examples: GI Yamagata, GI Hakusan, GI Nada Gogo

styles.name: Doburoku (どぶろく) — Unstrained Rice Brew
styles.impression: The unstrained ancestor of sake — thick, porridge-like, actively fermenting, and legally not sake at all.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water, fermented and consumed without pressing or straining.
styles.comments: Because it is never filtered it falls outside the seishu definition and is taxed as 'other brewed liquor' (その他の醸造酒). Home production remains illegal in Japan, but designated doburoku tokku — special deregulation zones established from 2002 — allow licensed farm and inn producers to make and sell it, which has driven a rural revival. Typically served fresh, sweet-sour and lightly effervescent.
styles.history: The pre-modern village and shrine brew; suppressed as home brewing was criminalised under the Meiji tax regime.
styles.examples: Farm-inn doburoku from deregulation zones; shrine festival brews

styles.name: Amazake (甘酒) — Non-Alcoholic Koji Drink
styles.impression: Saccharified rice without fermentation — sweet, thick, and useful to brewers as a koji reference point.
styles.ingredients: Rice and rice koji held warm (around 55–60 °C) until amylases convert the starch to glucose; or, in the cheaper version, sake lees plus sugar and water.
styles.comments: Included here because it isolates the enzymatic half of sake production. Holding koji at 55–60 °C runs saccharification without yeast — the mash goes sweet and stops. It demonstrates why sake reaches such high alcohol: in the real mash the same enzymes run continuously alongside the yeast, feeding it sugar slowly enough that it is never osmotically shocked. The koji-only version is alcohol-free; the sake-lees version carries residual alcohol, typically under 1%.
styles.history: Recorded in the Nihon Shoki as amanotamuzake; a traditional summer restorative and New Year drink.

legalStandards.title: Southeast Asia: Rice Ferments, Palm Toddy & Their Spirits
legalStandards.attribution: Southeast Asia ferments glutinous rice and palm sap with mixed-mould starter cakes (ragi/bubod/loog-pang) into a spectrum of sweet pastes, cloudy wines and clear distillates. Mostly traditional with little statutory definition; lambanog and some rice wines are commercially produced. Documented from ethnographic and food-science sources; values are typical.

styles.name: Tapai / Tapuy (Fermented Rice)
styles.impression: Sweet, sour and lightly alcoholic fermented glutinous rice (or cassava) — eaten as a dessert paste or drunk as it liquefies into rice wine.
styles.comments: Tapai ubi (cassava) and tapai pulut (rice) across Malaysia/Indonesia; tapuy in the Philippines. The liquid that collects is the rice wine; the solids are eaten. A close analogue to the Chinese jiuniang.
styles.ingredients: Steamed glutinous rice (or cassava) inoculated with ragi/bubod — a starter cake of Amylomyces mould and yeast that saccharifies and ferments at once.
styles.tags: seasia, tapai, tapuy, ragi, rice, traditional

styles.name: Brem / Rice Wine (Bali)
styles.impression: Balinese fermented glutinous (often black) rice wine — sweet, reddish-brown, low-to-moderate strength, used in offering and refreshment.
styles.comments: Brem Bali is bottled commercially. A solid brem cake is also sold as a snack.
styles.ingredients: Black or white glutinous rice fermented with ragi tapai starter; the liquid is aged.

styles.name: Sato / Lao Hai / Rice Wine of the Mekong
styles.impression: Thai and Lao fermented sticky-rice wine — sweet-sour and cloudy, the sipped 'jar wine' drunk communally through long reeds from a fermentation pot.
styles.comments: Sato is the Thai bottled version; lao hai is the communal jar. A parallel to Himalayan tongba and chhaang.
styles.ingredients: Steamed glutinous rice with loog-pang (Thai) or similar starter, fermented in a jar; water is added and the wine sipped through bamboo straws (lao hai).
styles.tags: thailand, laos, sato, rice-wine, jar-wine, traditional

styles.name: Tuba (Palm Toddy)
styles.impression: Philippine and Southeast Asian coconut palm toddy — sweet and fresh when tapped, souring through the day; sometimes reddened with barok (mangrove bark tannin).
styles.comments: Widespread across the Philippines and the Pacific. Aged tuba becomes vinegar (suka); distilled it becomes lambanog.
styles.ingredients: Coconut palm sap, wild-fermented; barok bark may be added for colour, tannin and preservation.

styles.name: Lambanog (Coconut Arrack)
styles.impression: The Philippine 'coconut vodka' — a clear, potent distillate of coconut toddy, smooth and neutral to fruity, now bottled in flavoured commercial lines.
styles.comments: A regional craft spirit of Quezon province, increasingly exported. Traditionally sold in recycled bottles at rural markets.
styles.ingredients: Fermented coconut toddy (tuba), pot-distilled, sometimes twice.

legalStandards.title: Spirits: Legal Definitions & Standards of Identity
legalStandards.attribution: Unlike beer, mead, and cider, distilled spirits have no judging style guidelines — but they do have binding legal definitions. This edition compiles the actual statutory standards of identity: the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 (UK), the Irish Whiskey Technical File, US 27 CFR Part 5 (TTB), EU Regulation 2019/787, Mexico's NOM-006/NOM-070, French AOC decrees, and equivalent national standards. Figures are the legal minima/maxima, not sensory targets. Compiled for reference; always check the current regulation for the jurisdiction you are producing in.

styles.name: Single Malt Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky distilled at a single Scottish distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills, matured in Scotland in oak.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley only. No other cereals. Yeast; fermentation by endogenous enzyme systems only.
styles.comments: Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: distilled below 94.8% ABV; matured in oak casks not exceeding 700 litres, in Scotland, for at least 3 years; bottled at no less than 40% ABV. The only permitted additions are water and plain caramel colouring (E150A). Age statements must refer to the youngest whisky in the bottle.
styles.history: Protected UK geographical indication; the modern legal framework dates to the 1988 Scotch Whisky Act, consolidated in the 2009 Regulations.

styles.name: Single Grain Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Scotch distilled at a single distillery from malted barley plus other whole cereals, typically in continuous column stills.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley, and whole grains of other cereals (commonly wheat or maize).
styles.comments: Same core Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 requirements as single malt — <94.8% ABV off the still, ≥3 years in oak ≤700 L in Scotland, ≥40% ABV bottling. 'Single' denotes one distillery, not one cask or one grain.

styles.name: Blended Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: A blend of one or more single malt Scotch whiskies with one or more single grain Scotch whiskies.
styles.comments: The dominant Scotch category by volume. All component whiskies must independently meet the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009. Blended Malt = malts only from multiple distilleries; Blended Grain = grains only from multiple distilleries.
styles.examples: Johnnie Walker, Chivas Regal, Famous Grouse

styles.name: Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: Whiskey distilled and matured on the island of Ireland; often triple-distilled and comparatively light.
styles.ingredients: Cereal grains; malted barley providing the enzymes.
styles.comments: Irish Whiskey Technical File (EU GI): distilled to less than 94.8% ABV; matured in wooden casks not exceeding 700 litres for at least 3 years on the island of Ireland; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Only water and plain caramel may be added.
styles.history: Protected EU geographical indication covering both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.

styles.name: Single Pot Still Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: The distinctive Irish style: a mixed mash of malted and unmalted barley pot-distilled at a single distillery, giving a characteristic creamy, spicy texture.
styles.ingredients: A mash of at least 30% malted barley and at least 30% unmalted barley; up to 5% other cereals permitted.
styles.comments: Defined in the Irish Whiskey Technical File. The unmalted barley — historically a response to 19th-century malt taxation — is what produces the category's signature mouthfeel.
styles.examples: Redbreast, Green Spot, Powers John's Lane

styles.name: Canadian Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky mashed, distilled and matured in Canada; historically rye-influenced and often light-bodied.
styles.comments: Canadian Food and Drug Regulations (B.02.020): mashed, distilled and aged in Canada; aged at least 3 years in small wood (≤700 L); bottled at ≥40% ABV. Uniquely, caramel and flavouring may be added — and up to 9.09% of another spirit may be blended in (the '9.09% rule'), which is why some Canadian whisky contains a small proportion of US bourbon or wine spirit.
styles.comparison: Often labelled 'rye' in Canada regardless of actual rye content, unlike US rye whiskey which requires ≥51% rye.

styles.name: Japanese Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky made in Japan, historically modelled on Scotch practice.
styles.comments: Japan had no binding legal definition until the Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association standard took effect in 2021 (voluntary, industry self-regulation): malted grain must be used, water must be extracted in Japan, saccharification/fermentation/distillation must occur at a Japanese distillery, distillation below 95% ABV, maturation ≥3 years in wooden casks ≤700 L in Japan, and bottling in Japan at ≥40% ABV. Products not meeting this may still legally be sold as Japanese-made whisky, so labels warrant scrutiny.

styles.name: Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: America's flagship whiskey: corn-dominant, aged in new charred oak, sweet and full.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to no more than 80% ABV (160 proof); entered into the barrel at no more than 62.5% ABV (125 proof); stored in NEW charred oak containers; bottled at no less than 40% ABV (80 proof). No colouring, flavouring or other blending materials may be added. There is no minimum ageing period for plain 'bourbon' — but see Straight Bourbon.
styles.history: Bourbon may be produced anywhere in the United States, not only Kentucky — a common misconception.
styles.examples: Buffalo Trace, Maker's Mark, Wild Turkey

styles.name: Straight Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon that has met a minimum maturation period.
styles.comments: All bourbon requirements plus storage in new charred oak for at least 2 years. If aged less than 4 years, the label must carry an age statement. 'Bottled in Bond' is stricter still (Standards of Fill / 27 CFR 5.88): the product of one distillation season by one distiller at one distillery, aged ≥4 years in a federally bonded warehouse, and bottled at exactly 50% ABV (100 proof).
styles.examples: Knob Creek, Elijah Craig, Henry McKenna Bottled-in-Bond

styles.name: Rye Whiskey (US)
styles.impression: Spicier, drier counterpart to bourbon.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% rye.
styles.comments: Identical distillation, barrel-entry and bottling limits to bourbon (≤80% ABV distillation, ≤62.5% ABV barrel entry, new charred oak, ≥40% ABV bottling). 'Straight Rye' requires ≥2 years.
styles.comparison: Contrast Canadian 'rye', which carries no rye-content requirement.

styles.name: Corn Whiskey
styles.impression: The legal ancestor of 'moonshine' — a corn-dominant whiskey that need not see new charred oak.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 80% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to ≤80% ABV. Uniquely, if aged at all it must be in UNUSED uncharred oak or USED barrels, and entered at ≤62.5% ABV. It may also be sold unaged. This is the category most 'white whiskey' and commercial 'moonshine' is legally bottled under.
styles.comparison: 'Moonshine' is not itself a federal standard of identity. Commercially it is sold either as corn whiskey, as unaged whisky, or — if distilled above 95% ABV from sugar — as neutral spirits or a specialty/flavoured product.

styles.name: Tennessee Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon-spec whiskey charcoal-mellowed before barrelling.
styles.comments: Tennessee Code § 57-2-106 and the NAFTA/USMCA designation: must meet all bourbon requirements, be produced in Tennessee, and be filtered through maple charcoal before ageing — the Lincoln County Process. Prichard's holds a statutory exemption from the charcoal step.

styles.name: American Single Malt Whiskey
styles.impression: The newest US standard of identity: 100% malted barley from a single American distillery.
styles.ingredients: 100% malted barley.
styles.comments: Formalised by TTB in 2024 (27 CFR 5.144): mashed, distilled and matured in the United States at a single distillery; distilled to ≤80% ABV; matured in oak casks ≤700 L; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Unlike bourbon, the oak need not be new or charred.

styles.name: Rum (US standard)
styles.impression: Spirit from sugarcane products, ranging from light and clean to heavy and estery.
styles.ingredients: Sugarcane products — molasses, cane syrup, or cane juice.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled from fermented sugarcane products at less than 95% ABV (190 proof) in such a manner that it possesses the taste, aroma and characteristics generally attributed to rum; bottled at ≥40% ABV. US law imposes no ageing requirement and no maximum congener limits, which is why 'rum' spans an enormous stylistic range.

styles.name: Rum (EU standard)
styles.impression: EU-regulated cane spirit with tighter congener requirements than the US definition.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787 Annex I(1): produced exclusively from molasses, cane syrup or cane juice; distilled at less than 96% ABV; minimum 225 g/hL of volatile substances at 100% ABV (a congener floor the US lacks); minimum 37.5% ABV. No added ethanol; sweetening only for rounding-off.
styles.comparison: The congener minimum means an EU 'rum' cannot be as neutral as some US-market products.

styles.name: Rhum Agricole (AOC Martinique)
styles.impression: Grassy, vegetal cane spirit distilled from fresh juice rather than molasses.
styles.ingredients: Fresh sugarcane juice only — never molasses.
styles.comments: AOC Martinique (1996): designated parcels on Martinique, specified cane varieties, fermentation without additives, single-column creole distillation to 65–75% ABV, bottled at ≥40%. Blanc rested ≥3 months; Élevé sous bois ≥12 months in oak; Vieux ≥3 years in oak ≤650 L.
styles.history: The style arose when 19th-century beet-sugar competition left cane juice available for direct distillation.

styles.name: Cachaça
styles.impression: Brazil's national spirit — fresh cane juice distilled to a comparatively low strength, retaining fruity and grassy character.
styles.ingredients: Fermented fresh sugarcane juice.
styles.comments: Brazilian Decree 6.871/2009 and MAPA Instruction 13/2005: produced in Brazil; distilled to 38–48% ABV (note the low maximum, which preserves congeners); up to 6 g/L sugar, or up to 30 g/L if labelled 'adoçada' (sweetened). Recognised as a distinctive product of Brazil by the US since 2013.

styles.name: Tequila
styles.impression: Cooked-agave spirit from designated Mexican regions, ranging from bright and peppery to oak-rounded.
styles.ingredients: Agave tequilana Weber, blue variety. '100% de agave' uses only agave sugars; 'mixto' permits up to 49% non-agave sugars.
styles.comments: NOM-006-SCFI-2012 and the Denominación de Origen: may be produced only in Jalisco and designated municipalities of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas. Bottled at 35–55% ABV. Classes by ageing: Blanco (unaged or <2 months), Joven/Oro (blended or lightly aged), Reposado (≥2 months in oak), Añejo (≥1 year in oak ≤600 L), Extra Añejo (≥3 years).

styles.name: Mezcal
styles.impression: Agave spirit traditionally roasted in earthen pits, typically smoky and highly variable by species and maker.
styles.ingredients: Any agave species permitted by the standard — espadín, tobalá, tepeztate, madrecuishe and many others — not restricted to blue Weber.
styles.comments: NOM-070-SCFI-2016: produced in designated states including Oaxaca, Guerrero, Durango, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, Michoacán, Puebla, Guanajuato and Tamaulipas. Bottled 35–55% ABV, always 100% agave. Three production classes: Mezcal (industrial methods permitted), Mezcal Artesanal (pit roasting, stone/wood milling, wood or clay stills), and Mezcal Ancestral (clay pot stills, most traditional throughout).
styles.comparison: All tequila is technically a mezcal in the historical sense, but the two now hold separate denominations of origin.

styles.name: Raicilla & Bacanora
styles.impression: Regional Mexican agave spirits with their own denominations of origin.
styles.comments: Bacanora (NOM-168, Sonora, from Agave angustifolia/pacífica) and Raicilla (DO granted 2019, Jalisco/Nayarit, from Agave maximiliana and others) were long produced informally — bacanora was outright prohibited in Sonora from 1915 to 1992 — and are now legally protected categories.

styles.name: Cognac
styles.impression: Double-distilled French grape brandy of great finesse, oak-matured.
styles.ingredients: Predominantly Ugni Blanc, with Folle Blanche and Colombard permitted.
styles.comments: AOC Cognac: grapes grown and distilled within the Charente/Charente-Maritime crus; double distillation in a copper alambic charentais, off the still at no more than 72.4% ABV; matured in French oak; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Age grades count from 1 April following harvest: VS ≥2 years, VSOP ≥4 years, Napoléon ≥6 years, XO ≥10 years (raised from 6 in 2018).

styles.name: Armagnac
styles.impression: Gascon grape brandy, typically column-distilled once and more rustic and aromatic than Cognac.
styles.comments: AOC Armagnac (Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze, Haut-Armagnac): usually continuous distillation in the alambic armagnacais to a lower strength than Cognac, retaining more congeners; aged in Gascon or Limousin oak; ≥40% ABV. Vintage (millésime) bottlings are a far more common tradition than in Cognac.

styles.name: Calvados
styles.impression: Norman apple (and pear) brandy.
styles.ingredients: Cider apples, and up to 30% pears depending on the appellation.
styles.comments: Three AOCs: Calvados, Calvados Pays d'Auge (double pot distillation, ≥2 years) and Calvados Domfrontais (≥30% pears, column distillation, ≥3 years). Base cider fermented without added sugar; minimum 2 years in oak; ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Pisco
styles.impression: Aromatic grape spirit from Peru or Chile — two distinct, legally separate products.
styles.comments: Peru (NTP 211.001): from eight permitted grape varieties in designated coastal regions; distilled to bottling strength with NO water added afterwards, no ageing in wood permitted (rest in inert vessels ≥3 months), 38–48% ABV. Chile's DO permits water reduction and oak. The two nations dispute the name internationally.
styles.examples: Barsol, Macchu Pisco (Peru); Alto del Carmen (Chile)

styles.name: Grappa & Pomace Brandy
styles.impression: Spirit distilled from grape pomace — skins, seeds and stems left after winemaking.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787: 'Grappa' is reserved for pomace of grapes produced and distilled in Italy (with parallel protections for Grappa di Ticino, Marc de Champagne, Bagaceira, Orujo, Tsipouro/Tsikoudia). Distilled at less than 86% ABV; ≥37.5% ABV bottling.

styles.name: Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-Vie
styles.impression: Unaged or lightly aged spirit distilled from whole fruit, prized for varietal aroma.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: fermented from fruit flesh (with stones where traditional); distilled at less than 86% ABV; no added alcohol, colouring or flavouring; ≥37.5% ABV. Protected examples include Kirsch, Mirabelle, Poire Williams, Slivovitz and Calvados' cousins. US law defines a parallel 'fruit brandy' at ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Gin
styles.impression: Neutral spirit flavoured with juniper as the dominant character.
styles.ingredients: Ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin plus juniper berries (Juniperus communis); other botanicals at the producer's discretion.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787 sets three tiers: 'Gin' (flavouring may be by any means, juniper predominant, ≥37.5% ABV); 'Distilled Gin' (redistilled with botanicals); and 'London Gin' (all flavour from redistillation of ethanol at ≥96% ABV with natural botanicals, no added colouring, sweetening ≤0.1 g/L, nothing added but water). US requires ≥40% ABV. Note that 'London Gin' is a method, not a place — it need not be made in London.

styles.name: Vodka
styles.impression: Spirit deliberately refined toward neutrality.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: ethanol of agricultural origin rectified so as to selectively reduce the organoleptic characteristics of the raw material; ≥37.5% ABV. US 27 CFR: treated with charcoal or otherwise so as to be without distinctive character, aroma, taste or colour; ≥40% ABV. The EU permits raw-material labelling; if made from anything other than cereals or potatoes, the base must be declared.

styles.name: Absinthe
styles.impression: High-strength anise and wormwood spirit, traditionally louching when diluted.
styles.ingredients: Grande wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), green anise, and fennel — the 'holy trinity'.
styles.comments: Absinthe has no harmonised EU spirit-category definition; it is regulated through thujone limits — EU: ≤35 mg/kg in bitter spirits; US TTB: 'thujone-free' meaning <10 ppm, and the label may not depict hallucinogenic or psychotropic effects. Switzerland's Absinthe/Fée Verte du Val-de-Travers holds a protected geographical indication. Typical bottling strength 45–74% ABV.
styles.history: Banned across much of Europe and the US in the early 20th century; legalised again in the EU from the 1990s and in the US in 2007.

styles.name: Aquavit / Akvavit
styles.impression: Scandinavian spirit dominated by caraway or dill.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: spirit drink flavoured with caraway seeds and/or dill seeds, distilled with botanicals; ≥37.5% ABV. Essential oils of other botanicals may contribute but caraway/dill must predominate. Norwegian Linie aquavit is traditionally matured in sherry casks shipped across the equator and back.

styles.name: Liqueur / Cordial
styles.impression: Sweetened flavoured spirit.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: minimum 100 g/L sugar (lower thresholds for cherry and gentian liqueurs); ≥15% ABV. US 27 CFR: 'cordial/liqueur' requires ≥2.5% sugar by weight and flavouring from natural materials; ≥30 proof (15% ABV). Crème de cassis requires ≥400 g/L sugar in the EU.

styles.name: Baijiu
styles.impression: China's national spirit and the world's most-consumed by volume — solid-state fermented grain spirit with intense, distinctive aromatics.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum most typically, often with rice, glutinous rice, wheat or corn; saccharified and fermented by qū (麴) starter cultures carrying moulds, yeasts and bacteria.
styles.comments: Governed by Chinese GB/T national standards, which classify baijiu by aroma type (香型) rather than by region: strong/thick aroma (nóngxiāng), light aroma (qīngxiāng), sauce aroma (jiàngxiāng), rice aroma (mǐxiāng) and around a dozen others. Solid-state fermentation in earthen pits or stone vessels distinguishes it from nearly all Western spirits.

styles.name: Shochu & Awamori
styles.impression: Japanese distilled spirit, typically single-distilled and lower in strength than Western spirits.
styles.ingredients: Barley (mugi), sweet potato (imo), rice (kome), buckwheat or brown sugar; saccharified with kōji mould.
styles.comments: Japanese Liquor Tax Act distinguishes honkaku (single-distilled, 'authentic', ≤45% ABV) from korui (multiply-distilled, ≤36% ABV). Awamori is the Okinawan variant, made from long-grain Thai indica rice with black kōji (Aspergillus luchuensis); aged awamori is called kūsū.

styles.name: Soju
styles.impression: Korea's dominant spirit; modern mass-market soju is diluted and lightly sweetened.
styles.comments: Korean Liquor Tax Act separates distilled soju (증류식, from grain, retaining congeners) from diluted soju (희석식, neutral spirit cut with water and flavourings) — the latter accounts for the overwhelming majority of sales, typically bottled at 16–25% ABV. Traditional Andong soju is distilled and considerably stronger.

styles.name: Arrack, Feni & Palm Spirits
styles.impression: South and Southeast Asian spirits from palm sap, cashew apple or cane.
styles.comments: Ceylon Arrack is distilled from fermented coconut palm flower sap and is protected as a Sri Lankan product. Feni holds a Goan GI: cashew feni from cashew-apple juice, coconut feni from palm toddy, traditionally triple-distilled in earthen pots. Batavia arrack (Java) is cane-based with red rice cakes added to fermentation.

styles.name: Unaged Grain Spirit / 'Moonshine'
styles.impression: Clear, unaged spirit from a grain or sugar wash — the untaxed tradition, now sold legally under existing categories.
styles.comments: 'Moonshine' is a cultural term, not a US standard of identity. To be labelled legally a product must fall into an existing class: Corn Whiskey (≥80% corn, ≤80% ABV distillation, unaged or in used/uncharred oak); unaged 'whisky' generally (grain mash, <95% ABV); Neutral Spirits/Vodka if distilled ≥95% ABV; or a 'Distilled Spirits Specialty' if sugar-based or flavoured. Historically the term denotes illicit, untaxed production — which remains a federal offence regardless of the recipe.
styles.comparison: Sugar-wash 'moonshine' cannot legally be called whiskey at all, since whiskey requires a grain mash.
styles.examples: Ole Smoky, Sugarlands (sold as corn whiskey or specialty)
styles.tags: moonshine, white dog, unaged, corn whiskey

legalStandards.title: Wine: Low-Intervention & Vessel Traditions
legalStandards.attribution: Wine made with as little technology as possible: fermented in buried clay rather than steel, on the yeast that came in on the grapes, with nothing added and nothing stripped out. These are methods that predate oenology and, in the natural-wine case, ones deliberately written to exclude it. Sourced to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage register, the Vin Méthode Nature charter lodged with the French fraud-control authority, and the OIV's international code. Only what those documents state is recorded here — none of them publishes gravity or ABV targets, so none is asserted. Other clay-vessel traditions (Portuguese vinho de talha, Spanish tinaja) are deliberately absent: their official specifications could not be retrieved, and describing their rules from wine-magazine coverage would not meet this archive's sourcing standard.

styles.name: Qvevri Wine (Georgia)
styles.impression: Wine fermented and aged in an egg-shaped earthenware vessel buried to its neck in the ground — the oldest continuously practised winemaking method still in commercial use, and the reference point for every modern amphora wine.
styles.comments: The qvevri is sealed and buried so the wine ferments underground for five to six months. Burial is temperature control without machinery: the earth holds the vessel steady through fermentation. No gravity or ABV figures are given here because UNESCO publishes none — it documents a living practice, not a product specification.
styles.history: Inscribed in 2013 (8.COM) on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Knowledge of both qvevri manufacture and qvevri winemaking is passed down within families and between neighbours and friends, with children learning by watching the communal harvest. Wine is integral to Georgian secular and religious life.
styles.ingredients: Grapes — and specifically not just the juice. UNESCO records that after pressing, the juice, grape skins, stalks and pips all go into the qvevri together.
styles.comparison: The direct ancestor of modern skin-contact and amphora wine. Where a contemporary winery buys a terracotta vessel as a stylistic choice, here it is the whole technology.
styles.tags: georgia, qvevri, kvevri, amphora, buried, skin-contact, unesco, intangible-heritage, low-intervention

styles.name: Skin-Contact ("Orange") White Wine
styles.impression: White grapes fermented on their skins like a red — giving tannin, grip and an amber-to-orange colour that white wine is not supposed to have.
styles.comments: Carries no separate numeric targets. Skin contact is a technique that spans many appellations and legal categories rather than a defined style with published specifications, and the length of contact — days to months — is the winemaker's choice, not a regulated figure.
styles.history: Not an invention of the modern natural-wine movement but the default before pressing-off became standard: the Georgian qvevri method, which UNESCO documents as fermenting juice together with skins, stalks and pips, is the same technique applied to white grapes.
styles.ingredients: White grapes fermented in contact with their own skins, and often stalks and pips.
styles.comparison: Made like a red wine from white grapes; the tannin comes from skin and pip contact, which is exactly what conventional white winemaking is designed to avoid.
styles.tags: orange-wine, skin-contact, amber, tannic-white, low-intervention, qvevri-descended

styles.name: Vin Méthode Nature (France)
styles.impression: France's defined natural-wine label — the rare case where 'natural wine' means something checkable rather than a marketing adjective, because the rules are written down and lodged with the fraud-control authority.
styles.comments: The charter is twelve numbered commitments, and the interesting ones are prohibitions: no inoculation of yeast or bacteria, no additives or processing aids, no voluntary modification of the structure of the grapes, and no interventionist physical techniques — reverse osmosis, filtration, thermovinification and centrifugation are named. A pied de cuve is the permitted way to start a ferment. Sulphites are the single exception, allowed only in small declared amounts in the finished wine and measured by the Frantz Paul method, with two logos distinguishing wines with no added sulphites from wines with an addition. The exact ceilings are deliberately not restated as a figure here: the published PDF does not extract its numerals reliably and the label's web page did not agree with it closely enough to assert one. No gravity or ABV is specified anywhere — the charter governs inputs and process, not the finished analysis.
styles.history: The Syndicat de défense des vins naturels lodged the charter with the DGCCRF, France's competition and fraud-control directorate, which validated it in 2020 — the first official French recognition of natural wine as a category. The text carried here is the English Charter of Commitment, updated January 2022.
styles.ingredients: 100% certified organic grapes (Nature & Progrès, or in the third year of conversion), hand-harvested. Inoculation of yeast OR bacteria is prohibited outright — the charter does not merely prefer indigenous yeast, it forbids adding any culture. No oenological additives or processing aids.
styles.comparison: Organic and biodynamic certification cover the vineyard; this covers the cellar, which is the part they leave open.
styles.tags: france, natural-wine, vin-methode-nature, no-inoculation, no-additives, low-sulphite, dgccrf, low-intervention

styles.name: Pét-Nat / Méthode Ancestrale
styles.impression: Sparkling wine made by bottling the wine before its first fermentation has finished, so the bubbles come from the original ferment completing under a crown cap — no tirage liqueur, no second fermentation, usually no disgorging.
styles.comments: Notably, this method sits outside the international standard. The OIV's sparkling-wine definitions recognise two production routes — secondary fermentation in bottle and secondary fermentation in closed tank — and define no ancestral or single-fermentation method among them. OIV does set the general threshold: a sparkling wine's excess carbon-dioxide pressure must be at least 3.5 bar at 20 °C, from CO2 of exclusively endogenous origin. That figure is a category definition, not a target for this style.
styles.history: The older method, predating the traditional/Champagne route of deliberately restarting a finished wine. Its modern revival travels under the abbreviation pét-nat, for pétillant naturel.
styles.ingredients: Grapes and nothing else — the point of the method is that no sugar or yeast is added to make it sparkle.
styles.comparison: The traditional method adds sugar and yeast to a finished base wine to start a second fermentation; here there is only ever one fermentation, interrupted by bottling.
styles.tags: pet-nat, methode-ancestrale, petillant-naturel, single-fermentation, low-intervention, oiv

fermentationArchetypes.label: Ale — clean cultured yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ale)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: A measured pitch of a single clean ale strain at ale temperatures. Pitch rate follows the beer model in the pitching calculator (cells/mL/°Plato).
specialHandling: Standard ~0.75 M cells/mL/°P target for ales — see the pitching calculator.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Lager — cold, high pitch
organisms: Saccharomyces pastorianus (lager)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Roughly double the ale pitch, fermented cold. The higher rate and low temperature keep esters down for a clean profile.
specialHandling: ~1.5 M cells/mL/°P; cold fermentation; diacetyl rest — see the pitching calculator.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Belgian / saison — warm, ester-forward
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Belgian/saison, POF+)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Deliberately expressive: warmer fermentation (and sometimes a lower pitch) to encourage the esters and phenols that define Belgian ales and saison.
specialHandling: Under-pitching and free-rising warm ferments raise ester/phenol production — the opposite goal to a clean lager.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Weissbier — banana & clove
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Weissbier, POF+)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: A POF-positive wheat-beer strain fermented warm; pitch rate and temperature are tuned to balance isoamyl-acetate (banana) against 4-vinyl-guaiacol (clove).
specialHandling: Lower pitch / warmer = more banana; higher pitch / cooler = more clove.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Mixed-culture / kettle sour
organisms: Saccharomyces
Brettanomyces
Lactobacillus
Pediococcus
fermentationArchetypes.approach: A deliberate blend (or sequential pitch) of yeast and souring bacteria — pitched, not spontaneous. Flanders reds/browns, American wild, and kettle sours sit here.
specialHandling: Souring bacteria added alongside or before Saccharomyces; long maturation for Brett character.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Spontaneous (lambic / coolship)
organisms: Enterobacteriaceae (Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Hafnia alvei) in the first month
Pediococcus damnosus with Saccharomyces cerevisiae and S. pastorianus from ~2 months
Dekkera (Brettanomyces) bruxellensis dominant from ~6 months, coexisting with P. damnosus
fermentationArchetypes.approach: No yeast is pitched. Cooled overnight in an open coolship, the wort is inoculated by ambient microbiota and matures in barrels over 1–3 years.

standard.metric: microbial succession, not a pitch rate
standard.note: Spitaels et al. (2014), from >2000 isolates over two years at a traditional Belgian lambic brewery: no yeast is pitched; ambient coolship inoculation drives a reproducible succession (Enterobacteriaceae → Pediococcus damnosus + Saccharomyces → Dekkera bruxellensis) over a 1–3 year maturation.

specialHandling: No pitch: hot wort cools overnight in an open coolship and is inoculated by the ambient microbiota of the Senne valley.
Characteristic succession — Enterobacteriaceae (first ~3–40 days) → Pediococcus damnosus + Saccharomyces (~2 months) → Dekkera bruxellensis (~6 months onward).
Matures in barrels 1–3 years before bottling; seasonal (cool months), with no controllable pitch rate.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Traditional opaque grain beer
organisms: Lactic acid bacteria: Limosilactobacillus (Lactobacillus) fermentum, Pediococcus acidilactici, Lactococcus lactis, Leuconostoc spp.
Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (dominant, 45–99% of the alcoholic phase)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: African sorghum/millet opaque beers and European farmhouse grain ferments: sour, low-alcohol, often back-slopped from a previous batch rather than pitched from a pure culture. Drunk actively fermenting.

standard.metric: two-stage spontaneous fermentation, not a pitch rate
standard.note: Sawadogo-Lingani et al. (2021, dolo): a lactic-acid souring of the wort (12–16 h; LAB to 8.8–9.9 log CFU/mL, pH ~3.0–3.8) is followed by an alcoholic fermentation (9–14 h) on indigenous Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Seeded by back-slopping — part of a previous batch, or a sun-dried yeast leaven — rather than a measured pitch.

specialHandling: Two stages: spontaneous lactic souring first, then alcoholic fermentation on indigenous yeast.
Back-slopping seeds the next batch — a portion of previous beer or a sun-dried yeast leaven acts as the local starter.
Drunk while actively fermenting; sour and low in alcohol.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Wine — active dry yeast, dosed by weight
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Winemakers dose active dry wine yeast by weight per volume of must — a different standard from beer's cells/mL/°Plato. The yeast is rehydrated warm before inoculation.

standard.metric: g active dry wine yeast per hectolitre of must
standard.note: AWRI: an inoculum of 0.25 g/L (25 g/hL) to achieve a minimum 5×10^6 viable cells/mL; rehydrate in 5–10× the yeast weight of 38–40 °C water, stand 10–15 min. Up to ~2× for highly clarified, high-Brix, or high-SO2 musts.

specialHandling: Rehydrate warm; a rehydration nutrient (inactivated yeast) improves survival in difficult musts.
Higher dose for clarified/high-Brix/high-SO2 juice.
fermentationArchetypes.comparison: Where beer counts cells/mL/°Plato, wine doses grams/hL — the same idea (enough viable cells) expressed in the winemaker's units.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Wine — native / spontaneous
organisms: Early non-Saccharomyces from the grape surface: Hanseniaspora, Starmerella, Pichia, Debaryomyces, Metschnikowia
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which takes over and finishes the ferment
fermentationArchetypes.approach: No yeast added; the must ferments on the vineyard/winery microbiota. A per-style choice within many wine categories rather than a separate legal class.

standard.metric: yeast succession; no pitch rate
standard.note: Zabukovec et al. (2020): spontaneous fermentation starts on the non-Saccharomyces yeasts that prevail on grape skins — Hanseniaspora, Starmerella, Pichia, Debaryomyces, Metschnikowia — which ferment sugar only weakly. Their exponential growth lasts just two to three days before they reach stationary phase, after which Saccharomyces cerevisiae, more ethanol-tolerant and able to grow anaerobically, dominates and completes the fermentation.

specialHandling: Higher risk and variability; the non-Saccharomyces early phase shapes aroma before Saccharomyces finishes.
That early phase is short — two to three days of exponential growth — but it is where higher alcohols, esters, terpenes and volatile thiols are laid down.
The indigenous population is what carries terroir character, which is the reason for not inoculating.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Biologically-aged (flor) wine
organisms: Film-forming Saccharomyces cerevisiae; historically classed as the four flor races beticus, cheresiensis, montuliensis and rouxii, now known to share a common origin
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Fino/manzanilla sherry: after fermentation a film (flor) of specialised yeast grows on the wine surface under a solera, ageing it oxidatively-protected.

standard.metric: biological ageing under a yeast film; minimum 15% vol
standard.note: OIV defines flor (film) wines as wines biologically aged in contact with air through the development of a film of typical yeasts on the free surface, AFTER complete alcoholic fermentation of the must — nothing is arrested. Wine spirit or neutral alcohol may be added, and the finished wine must reach at least 15% vol actual alcohol. Legras et al. (2016): the velum is an air–liquid biofilm that forms once fermentable carbon is exhausted; FLO11 expression at the diauxic shift raises cell-surface hydrophobicity, and the yeast switches from fermentative to oxidative metabolism, consuming ethanol, glycerol, acetic and lactic acid.

specialHandling: Aged after fermentation is complete — this is not an arrested ferment, unlike port-type fortification.
The velum forms on nutrient depletion: no fermentable carbon, with FLO11-driven cell-surface hydrophobicity floating the cells into a biofilm.
Metabolism turns oxidative — the film consumes the wine's own ethanol and glycerol rather than sugar.
Casks are left partly filled so the film has a free surface to grow on; Jerez ages these fractionally through a solera.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Sparkling — second fermentation (tirage)
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (bayanus/prise-de-mousse type)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: A base wine is re-fermented with added sugar and a robust yeast (liqueur de tirage) in bottle or tank to trap CO2; the classic method ages on lees.

standard.metric: second fermentation in a sealed vessel; regulated additions
standard.note: OIV International Code of Oenological Practices: the second fermentation is started by a tirage liqueur (sugar, must or concentrated must) plus a selected yeast inoculum, with clarifying agents (bentonite, organic fining agents, tannins, potassium alginate) and fermentation activators permitted. Nutritive salts are capped — diammonium phosphate or ammonium sulphate at a maximum 0.3 g/L expressed as the salt, and thiamin hydrochloride at a maximum 0.6 mg/L expressed as thiamin. The bottle route runs tirage, stacking, riddling, disgorging and dosage.

specialHandling: Alcohol-tolerant, flocculent yeast for the second ferment; lees ageing for autolytic character.
Nutrient additions are legally capped: 0.3 g/L DAP or ammonium sulphate, 0.6 mg/L thiamin.
The yeast has to start in a finished, alcoholic base wine, which is why a robust prise-de-mousse strain is used rather than a primary-fermentation strain.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Fortified — fermentation arrested by spirit
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Port-type wines: a normal wine ferment is stopped early by adding grape spirit, killing the yeast and leaving residual sweetness at a higher strength.

standard.metric: acquired alcoholic strength, % vol (liqueur wine)
standard.note: OIV defines fortification as the addition to wine of wine spirit, rectified alcohol of viticultural origin, or rectified food alcohol — and specifically discourages it for merely raising alcohol, permitting it to produce the special-wine categories (flor/film wines, fortified wines, mistelles). Liqueur wine is defined at an acquired alcoholic strength of at least 15% and at most 22% vol (states may allow up to 24% domestically), made from grape must — including partially fermented must — and/or wine with distillates, spirits and alcohol of vitivinicultural origin added.

specialHandling: Fermentation is deliberately halted mid-way; timing of the spirit addition sets sweetness.
The spirit must itself meet the OIV production conditions for wine spirit or rectified alcohol.
Distinct from flor wines, which are aged only after fermentation runs to completion.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Cider — cultured wine/cider yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine/cider active dry yeast)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Modern cider often pitches a cultured wine or cider yeast, frequently after sulphiting the juice to suppress wild flora — closer to the wine model than the beer one.

standard.metric: g active dry yeast per hectolitre of juice
standard.note: Scott Laboratories: 2 lb/1000 gal (25 g/hL) for a standard primary fermentation, rising to 2.8 lb/1000 gal (35 g/hL) for high-Brix juice above 25 °Bx. The same dose-by-weight standard as wine — AWRI gives 25 g/hL for a minimum 5×10⁶ viable cells/mL — so the inoculation calculator's g/hL model applies directly.

specialHandling: Dosed by weight per volume like wine, not by cells/mL/°Plato like beer.
Nutrient-poor apple juice benefits from yeast nutrient; cool, slow ferments preserve aroma.
Juice is commonly sulphited before pitching to suppress the wild flora the cultured yeast is meant to outcompete.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Cider — wild / keeved (traditional)
organisms: indigenous yeast and bacteria of the fruit and cellar
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Traditional French/Basque/English ciders ferment on wild flora; keeving deliberately starves the ferment (via a pectin gel, the chapeau brun) to leave natural sweetness. No pitch.

standard.metric: nutrient depletion by keeving; no pitch rate
standard.note: Januszek et al. (2024): keeving (défécation) adds calcium chloride and pectin methylesterase to the must. Demethylation of the homogalacturonan chain in pectin lets it bind calcium and form a gel, which CO₂ floats to the surface as the chapeau brun over roughly 2–6 days. Around 50% of the pectin and nutrients are trapped in that cap and the sediment beneath it; the resulting shortage of assimilable nitrogen makes the fermentation slow and stop of its own accord, leaving residual sweetness.

specialHandling: Keeving starves rather than stops: nutrient removal, not sulphite or filtration, is what arrests the ferment.
Calcium chloride plus pectin methylesterase drive gel formation; the chapeau brun rises within about 2–6 days.
Slow and low-temperature by design — the point is an incomplete fermentation with natural sweetness left in.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Mead — wine yeast + staggered nutrients
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Honey is nutrient-free, so mead pitches a wine yeast and manages fermentation through staggered nutrient additions rather than pitch rate alone. The builder computes a TOSNA-style schedule (lib/must.ts).
specialHandling: Staggered nutrient additions (TOSNA) over the first third of fermentation; without them, sluggish ferments and H2S.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Sake — kōji + sake yeast (multiple parallel fermentation)
organisms: Aspergillus oryzae (kōji, saccharification)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae — kyōkai sake yeast (kōbo, fermentation)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: A common misconception is that kōji ferments the sake. It does not: kōji mould saccharifies the rice (amylase/protease), while a SEPARATE sake yeast — usually a kyōkai strain from the Brewing Society of Japan, added via the shubo/moto starter — carries out the alcoholic fermentation. Both run at once in the moromi, 'multiple parallel fermentation', with rice, water and kōji added in three stages (sandan-jikomi).
specialHandling: Shubo/moto starter built first (sokujō fast-souring, or kimoto/yamahai slow lactic).
Kōji and yeast work simultaneously in the main mash.
fermentationArchetypes.comparison: Unlike beer (mash then pitch) or wine (crush then pitch), saccharification and fermentation happen together, which lets sake reach unusually high alcohol.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Huangjiu (Chinese yellow wine) — qū starter
organisms: Moulds of the qū: Aspergillus oryzae, Rhizopus oryzae, Mucor spp., Monascus purpureus
Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (the principal ethanol producer)
Bacteria: Lactobacillus spp., Bacillus spp., Weissella, Leuconostoc
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Chinese yellow rice wine uses a qū starter — a cake of grain colonised by a consortium of moulds, yeasts and bacteria — to saccharify and ferment together, related to but distinct from Japanese kōji.

standard.metric: semi-solid open fermentation; no pitch rate
standard.note: Tian et al. (2022): wheat qū supplies the amylase, protease and esterase that saccharify the starch while Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments the released sugars — simultaneous saccharification and alcoholic fermentation, termed semi-solid open fermentation. A typical course runs ~30 °C for 5–7 days, after which the mash is opened to drop to ~15 °C and held 1–2 months to finish.

specialHandling: Qū supplies both saccharifying enzymes and fermenting organisms.
Saccharification and alcoholic fermentation run simultaneously (semi-solid open fermentation), not in sequence.
Lactic acid bacteria dominate the bacterial community, and which species dominate tracks with product quality.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Korean rice wine — nuruk starter
organisms: Moulds of the nuruk: Aspergillus, Rhizopus and Mucor spp.
Yeasts: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (>90% of the fungal community through fermentation) and Saccharomycopsis fibuligera
Lactic acid bacteria: Lactilactobacillus curvatus, Liquorilactobacillus satsumensis, Pediococcus acidilactici
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Takju/makgeolli and yakju use nuruk, a traditional grain fermentation starter carrying both saccharifying moulds and yeast.

standard.metric: starter-culture ferment; no pitch rate
standard.note: Song et al. (2022): nuruk is made by natural solid fermentation of moistened ground rice or wheat, growing a mixed population of moulds, yeasts and lactic acid bacteria. Its moulds release amylase and glucoamylase to saccharify the rice while the yeasts ferment the released sugars. The gayangju course they followed ran ~25 °C for the fermentation stages, then ~15 °C for an aging period of about 35 days.

specialHandling: Nuruk carries both the saccharifying moulds and the fermenting yeasts — there is no separate yeast pitch in the traditional method.
Lactic acid bacteria persist throughout and shape the finished acidity.
Often a multi-stage build (a first and second fermentation) before an extended cool aging.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Southeast Asian rice ferment — ragi / starter cake
organisms: Amylolytic moulds: Amylomyces rouxii (some isolates reclassified as Mucor indicus), Rhizopus oryzae, Mucor spp.
Yeasts: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida utilis, Endomycopsis burtonii
Lactic acid bacteria: Pediococcus pentosaceus, Lactobacillus plantarum, L. fermentum
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Tapai and related SE-Asian rice ferments use ragi — a dried starter cake of amylolytic mould plus yeast — inoculated onto cooked rice.

standard.metric: starter-cake ferment; no pitch rate
standard.note: Delva et al. (2022): ragi tapai is a dry starter cake (~2.5 cm across, ~0.5 cm thick) of rice flour, spices and a mixed microbial culture. Amylomyces rouxii is the principal amylolytic organism, producing amyloglucosidase and growing on raw substrate. Two functional groups do the work — one breaks starch down to glucose, the other converts glucose to ethanol.

specialHandling: The starter is a physical cake crumbled over cooked rice, not a liquid pitch.
Two functional groups: amylolytic moulds saccharify the starch, yeasts ferment the glucose.
Related starters across the region go by different names — chu (China), ragi (Indonesia), ragi-tapai (Malaysia), bubod (Philippines), marcha (India), nuruk (Korea).

fermentationArchetypes.label: Whisky wash — congener-developing distiller's yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (distiller's / M-type; sometimes with brewer's yeast)
Lactic acid bacteria in the late fermentation — Lactobacillus spp., Leuconostoc spp.
fermentationArchetypes.approach: The wash is fermented for flavour, not clean neutrality: distillers pick strains and conditions that develop esters and higher alcohols (congeners), which carry through distillation into the spirit's character.

standard.metric: pitching temperature °C and fermentation duration
standard.note: Walker & Hill (2016): Scotch whisky washes normally have no temperature control — the wort is simply pitched at 16–19 °C and allowed to rise, typically peaking around 32–33 °C, over a 2–3 day fermentation. The wort is never boiled, so residual malt enzymes keep converting during fermentation (worth roughly 30% additional spirit). Over 100 esters form, mostly fruity; iso-amyl alcohol makes up 40–70% of the higher alcohols and turns unpleasant when too high. Most Scotch malt distilleries pitch commercially supplied cream yeast directly without propagation; grain distilleries pitch at much lower rates.

specialHandling: Warmer / more-stressed ferments and congener-forward strains raise esters; cooler, cleaner ferments reduce them.
The wash is unhopped and unboiled — malt enzymes carry on converting starch during fermentation.
A limited late lactic fermentation is deliberate craft, not contamination: LAB acids esterify to ethyl lactate and γ-dodecalactone, giving sweet, fruity and creamy notes.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Rum wash — osmophilic yeast + dunder
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (the usual production yeast)
Stress-tolerant non-Saccharomyces: Schizosaccharomyces pombe, plus Candida, Debaryomyces, Kluyveromyces, Pichia, Hanseniaspora
Bacteria: Lactobacillus spp. and Propionibacterium spp.
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Cane/molasses washes use osmophilic yeast; heavy 'high-ester' rums recycle dunder (stillage) in muck pits to build the acids and esters that define the style.

standard.metric: fermentation duration and temperature
standard.note: Mangwanda et al. (2021): rum fermentations run anywhere from 20 hours to 21 days — short 20–26 hour ferments give light rums, ferments beyond 7 days give heavy ones. Temperature is held at 28–35 °C for yeast growth; S. cerevisiae works best at 20–30 °C and commercial distilling strains tolerate 32–35 °C, with metabolic activity falling away rapidly above that. Molasses is a harsh, low-water-activity substrate (S. cerevisiae needs a water activity of at least 0.65), so few organisms besides Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Bacillus subtilis survive alongside it. Dunder — the volatile-depleted liquid left in the still from previous batches — is routinely added back to preserve volatiles and organoleptic continuity between batches.

specialHandling: Dunder/muck concentrates esters and acids; long, warm, deliberately funky ferments.
Fermentation length is the main lever on style: hours for light rum, over a week for heavy.
Bacteria are part of the flavour, not just spoilage — Lactobacillus and Propionibacterium give 2,3-butanediol, diacetyl and propionic acid, though too much inhibits the ferment.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Neutral spirit wash — low-congener yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (low-congener / vodka-type)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Vodka, gin base and neutral spirit want the opposite of whisky: a low-metabolite yeast and clean conditions that minimise congeners for a neutral distillate. Higher fermentation temperature tends to lower esters and raise higher alcohols.
specialHandling: Low-congener strain; controlled temperature to minimise flavour compounds.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Brandy — wine base, then distil
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Grape and fruit brandies ferment as wine first (wine yeast, wine handling) and are then distilled; the fermentation archetype is the wine one, with distillation added.

standard.metric: g active dry wine yeast per hectolitre of must
standard.note: The base is a wine, so the wine standard governs the fermentation: AWRI's 25 g/hL of active dry wine yeast to reach a minimum 5×10⁶ viable cells/mL, rehydrated in 5–10× the yeast weight of 38–40 °C water. What distinguishes this archetype is what happens after — the wine is distilled rather than bottled, and it is made as a distillation base rather than as a drinking wine.

specialHandling: Follow the wine-cultured approach — this is the wine model with a still on the end.
Base wines for distillation are conventionally made with minimal sulphite; treat that as practice rather than a sourced figure here.
A spontaneous base wine follows the wine-native succession instead.
fermentationArchetypes.comparison: Same fermentation as wine-cultured; the difference is downstream, not in the ferment.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Agave spirits — cultured or wild
organisms: Yeasts: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Hanseniaspora spp., Candida spp., Torulaspora delbrueckii, Kluyveromyces marxianus
Bacteria: lactic acid bacteria, Leuconostoc mesenteroides
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Cooked-agave musts are fermented either with a cultured yeast (industrial tequila) or on wild/ambient flora in open wooden vats (traditional mezcal), which drives much of the rustic character.

standard.metric: spontaneous fermentation duration, days
standard.note: Becerra-Lucio et al. (2022): agave piñas are cooked in earthen pit ovens or autoclaves, which both sterilises the material and hydrolyses its complex carbohydrates into fermentable sugars — but inoculation begins the moment the oven is opened, via hands, tools and the surrounding environment. Artisanal mezcal is therefore spontaneous, not pitched, and takes roughly 8 to 20 days. Non-Saccharomyces yeasts and bacteria supply the higher alcohols, acetate esters and ethyl esters behind its floral and fruity character.

specialHandling: Open-air wild ferments for traditional styles; strain choice for industrial.
Cooking does the saccharification — there is no enzyme or starter culture, the agave's own fructans are hydrolysed by heat.
The 'inoculum' is the production environment itself: the consortium comes from the surroundings once the oven is opened.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Baijiu — Daqu/Xiaoqu, solid-state fermentation
organisms: Fungi: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Kazachstania, Aspergillus, Rhizopus, Apiotrichum
Bacteria: Lactobacillus (organic acids), Bacillus (pyrazines and aromatic compounds), Clostridium (caproic-acid precursors)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Baijiu is made by solid-state fermentation of grain with a qū starter (Daqu or Xiaoqu) — a self-sustaining microbial consortium — often in earthen pits, then solid-state distilled. Not a single pitched yeast.

standard.metric: solid-state fermentation on a qū consortium; no pitch rate
standard.note: Tu et al. (2022): Daqu is a grain starter of wheat, barley and/or peas, classed by the temperature it is made at — high-temperature for sauce (Maotai) aroma, medium for strong aroma, low for light aroma. Xiaoqu is a simpler rice/sorghum/barley starter made with Chinese medicinal herbs, suited to southern China, and in xiaoqu baijiu saccharification and fermentation run at the same time. In traditional production the organisms come from the environment, the workers and the jiuqu itself rather than a deliberate pitch; modern practice may add isolated functional strains. For strong-aroma baijiu the earthen pit is essential — Clostridium spp. living in the pit mud produce caproic acid and ethyl caproate.

specialHandling: Solid-state, pit/vessel-dependent microbiota; aroma type (香型) follows the qū and process.
The pit itself is part of the organism set — pit-mud Clostridium is what makes strong-aroma baijiu taste the way it does.
Daqu type is chosen by the aroma target: high-temperature daqu for sauce aroma, medium for strong, low for light.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Distilled milk liquor (arkhi)
organisms: Lactic acid bacteria: Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens (tarag base), L. helveticus, Lactococcus lactis
Lactose-fermenting yeasts: Kluyveromyces marxianus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Central Asian milk liquor distils fermented mare's/cow's milk (airag/kumis): the lactose is fermented by a kefir-type yeast-and-bacteria culture, then distilled.

standard.metric: fermented-milk base, then distilled; no pitch rate
standard.note: Kumar et al. (2025): arkhi is a distilled alcoholic beverage derived from fermented milk, with tarag — a firm Mongolian yoghurt made by fermenting boiled and cooled cow's or goat's milk with Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens, reaching pH 3.6–3.9 — as its base. The related airag is horse or camel milk agitated vigorously in leather sacks or wooden containers for one to two days on Lactobacillus helveticus, Lactococcus lactis and native yeasts, reaching 1–3% ethanol. Distillation concentrates that low-alcohol milk ferment; there is no pitch rate, the culture is carried over from a previous batch.

specialHandling: Back-slopped milk culture; lactose (not maltose/sucrose) is the sugar.
The base ferment is weak (1–3% ABV), so distillation is what makes it a spirit at all.
Acidity is high going into the still — the tarag base sits at pH 3.6–3.9.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Regional traditional spirits
organisms: varies by tradition (wild or local starter)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Feni, palm distillates and other regional spirits ferment on local wild flora or a regional starter before distillation; handled per style rather than one rule.
specialHandling: Map per style as primary sources are secured.
This is deliberately a catch-all, not a technique: it groups unrelated traditions (Goan feni, Southeast Asian palm distillates, Korean regional liquors) that share only the fact of being distilled.

It stays marked pending on purpose — no single source can honestly describe all of them, and the right unit of sourcing is the individual style. Where a tradition is well documented it gets its own archetype instead.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Spontaneous sap/juice ferment (palm wine, pulque, chicha)
organisms: wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Zymomonas mobilis, plus non-Saccharomyces yeasts and lactic acid bacteria
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Palm sap (palm wine), agave sap (pulque) and maize (chicha) ferment spontaneously on the microbes already present in the sap and environment — no yeast is added. In palm wine, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Zymomonas mobilis are the main alcohol producers.
specialHandling: Very fast (hours to a day); the microbial mix shifts continuously and drives the flavour.
Traditionally drunk fresh, still fermenting.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Fermented milk (airag / kumis / kefir)
organisms: Lactic acid bacteria: Lactobacillus helveticus (dominant), Lactococcus lactis, Leuconostoc mesenteroides
Lactose-fermenting yeasts: Kluyveromyces marxianus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Mildly alcoholic fermented milks are back-slopped from a living culture of lactic bacteria and yeast that ferment lactose — a starter culture, not a pitched pure strain.

standard.metric: back-slopped mixed LAB + yeast ferment; % ethanol
standard.note: Martuzzi et al. (2024): mare-milk fermentation is a bacteria–yeast interaction — LAB acidify the milk while the yeasts modify titratable acidity — and is started by back-slopping, inoculating fresh milk with a small quantity of already-fermented milk as the natural starter. Koumiss generally contains about 2% alcohol, 0.5–1.5% lactic acid, 2–4% sugar and 2% fat; Russian classification runs weak (0.7–1% ethanol), normal (1–1.75%) and strong (1.75–2.5%). Kumar et al. (2025) describe airag as horse or camel milk agitated vigorously in leather sacks or wooden containers for one to two days, giving a slightly effervescent drink at 1–3% ethanol.

specialHandling: Back-slopping maintains the culture; simultaneous souring and light alcohol.
The sugar is lactose, so the yeast has to be a lactose fermenter — Kluyveromyces marxianus, not a brewing strain.
Agitation is part of the method: vigorous stirring in a leather sack or wooden vessel aerates the milk and drives the ferment.

fermentationArchetypes.label: SCOBY ferment (kombucha)
organisms: Acetic acid bacteria: Acetobacter aceti, Komagataeibacter xylinum, Gluconobacter oxydans, Acetobacter pasteurianus
Yeasts: Brettanomyces/Dekkera, Zygosaccharomyces, Saccharomyces, Schizosaccharomyces pombe
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Kombucha ferments sweetened tea with a SCOBY — a symbiotic pellicle of acetic-acid bacteria and yeast added from a previous batch (with starter liquid), not a measured yeast pitch.

standard.metric: back-slopped SCOBY plus starter liquid; days
standard.note: Ojo & de Smidt (2023): the SCOBY is a metabolically active symbiotic community of bacteria and yeast that builds a jelly-like cellulose pellicle (zooglea biofilm) at the liquid–air interface. A representative protocol dissolves 50 g sucrose in 1 L boiling water, steeps tea for 5 minutes, cools to 20 °C, then inoculates with 24 g of SCOBY plus 0.2 L of previously fermented kombucha — the starter liquid lowers pH to shut out unwanted microbes. Optimal fermentation runs 6–14 days. The symbiosis is a loop: yeast ethanol lets the bacteria make acetic acid, and that acetic acid stimulates the yeast to make more ethanol.

specialHandling: Low alcohol; the bacteria oxidise ethanol to acid, giving the sour profile.
The back-slopped starter liquid matters as much as the pellicle — it acidifies the tea immediately and keeps contaminants out.
Composition varies with substrate, origin, climate and production conditions, so no two SCOBYs are the same culture.

fermentationArchetypes.label: Wild / back-slopped grain & folk ferments
organisms: Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Lactic acid bacteria: Lactobacillus casei, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei, Leuconostoc mesenteroides
Acetic acid bacteria: Acetobacter pasteurianus (bread kvass)
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Kvass, tesgüino and other folk grain ferments run on wild flora, often back-slopped, and are drunk young and lightly alcoholic. Handled per tradition.

standard.metric: combined lactic and alcoholic fermentation; % ethanol
standard.note: Ashaolu & Reale (2020): kvass is made from fermented barley and rye malt, rye flour and stale rye bread, mainly in Russia, Poland and the Baltic states. It is a combined lactic and alcoholic fermentation on a natural mixed flora of Saccharomyces cerevisiae with lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus casei and Leuconostoc mesenteroides — no pure culture is pitched, and species composition varies widely with technique and medium. It contains 1% alcohol or less, and because it is not pasteurised the live LAB remain in the finished drink.

specialHandling: Back-slopping; short, low-alcohol ferments.
Lactic and alcoholic fermentation run together — the sourness is not a fault, it is half the process.
Species composition is genuinely variable between makers; this archetype describes a practice, not a fixed culture.

fermentationArchetypes.label: No yeast added (pruno)
organisms: whatever is present — wild and from added bread; uncontrolled
fermentationArchetypes.approach: Improvised prison wine adds no cultured yeast; fermentation relies on wild organisms and any bread thrown in. It is included as a warning, not a method: pruno has caused documented botulism outbreaks.
specialHandling: No pitch, no control; genuine public-health hazard — see the pruno guideline entry.
